title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
text:
Goal: you will explain why a one-line change to a notebook produces a noisy diff, and name four ways to make the change reviewable.
Before you start: Save Point (for git diff), and two tiny mock notebooks, before.ipynb and after.ipynb (about 2.5 KB each). They are mock files that omit cell ids, so they are not strictly valid nbformat 4.5. Save both into an empty folder.
Time: about 15 minutes.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
section: A notebook is a JSON file
text:
A notebook is a JSON file
A .ipynb file is a JSON document with metadata, nbformat, nbformat_minor (the notebook file-format version numbers) and a list of cells. A code cell stores its source, and also an execution_count and its outputs. A plot is stored inside the file as a base64 string (the image bytes written out as plain text). Source and outputs share one file, so any run rewrites lines next to the code.
This is what git sees, with or without an agent. The two mock notebooks differ by one real change: the cutoff 30 became 40. Compare them:
diff before.ipynb after.ipynb
5c5
<    "execution_count": 3,
---
>    "execution_count": 7,
8c8
<     "print(len([r for r in reads if r >= 30]))"
---
>     "print(len([r for r in reads if r >= 40]))"
15c15
<       "3\n"
---
>       "2\n"
21c21
<       "image/png": "AAECAwQFBgcICQoLDA0ODxAREhMUFRYXGBkaGx...
---
>       "image/png": "AAMGCQwPEhUYGx4hJCcqLTAzNjk8P0JFSEtOUV...
Four spots changed, and one of them is the code. The rest is the run counter, the printed result and an image blob. A real notebook has more cells and bigger images, so the code change is harder still to find; git diff --stat shows how large a notebook diff is.
The risk is the same with a coding agent as with a human: a reviewer who cannot find the code change may approve without reading it.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
section: Four ways to make changes reviewable
text:
Four ways to make changes reviewable
Each option moves the noise somewhere else. Pick by what your team can adopt.

nbstripout: strips outputs and some metadata when git stores the notebook. Outputs stay in your working file. Cost: each collaborator runs nbstripout --install themselves, because git cannot set up the filter on clone.
jupytext: pairs the .ipynb with a .py (the py:percent format suits code). You review the .py and outputs stay in the .ipynb. Cost: two files to keep in sync.
nbdime: a notebook-aware diff, with nbdiff in the terminal, nbdiff-web in the browser, git integration and a merge driver. Cost: everyone reviewing needs it installed.
marimo: stores notebooks as pure Python, so ordinary git diffs work. Cost: a different notebook tool from Jupyter. marimo convert your_notebook.ipynb > your_notebook.py converts an existing notebook.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
text:
Review the code cells
Whatever you choose, the review habit is the same:

Look at the source cells. Treat outputs as something to regenerate.
Run git diff --stat before committing and look for a notebook that grew by megabytes.
An output in a diff shows that something ran once; a re-run shows whether the code produces it.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
text:
With a companion

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Claude Code reads a .ipynb with all its cells and outputs, and an output-heavy notebook fills the context window (the text the agent can hold at once). It edits notebooks with NotebookEdit, one cell at a time, by cell_id. Replacing a code cell clears that cell’s execution count and saved outputs, so the agent’s diff contains lost outputs as well as new source.
nbstripout is a git filter, so outputs stay in the working file and the agent still reads them. To keep the agent on the code, strip outputs from the working copy (nbstripout’s pre-commit mode does this) or point the agent at the paired .py. Check the docs for your version.


The idea is the same: review the source cells. Check OpenCode’s docs for how it handles notebook files.

You will also be on the receiving end of LLM-assisted work. Reviewing it is the same craft as any review, with a few shifts in attention.

title: The Reviewer’s Code

Formats that review well
Notebooks show the difference well. A marimo notebook is stored as a plain .py file, so a diff shows what changed. A Jupyter .ipynb is JSON that also stores outputs and run counts, so diffs are noisy and hard to read, though stripping tools exist. When you ask an agent to produce analysis, choose a format your reviewer can diff.

title: Send Small, Say So
text:
Goal: you will hand work to collaborators, whether or not they use LLMs, without passing them your review burden.
Before you start: Spot the Mirage.
Time: about 15 minutes.
A reef is a community. The Review-leech feeds on the cost of checking an agent’s output when it lands on the next person without a word. Four habits starve it.
These habits help every reviewer. A colleague who does not use LLMs can review your work without learning a tool.

title: Send Small, Say So
section: When you worry about looking lazy
text:
When you worry about looking lazy
A common worry is that people will think you are lazy or unoriginal for using an agent. Make the facts easy to see.

Say plainly what the agent did and what you checked. “The agent drafted the plotting code. I read it and compared the output with a hand calculation.”
Follow your team’s norm. Some groups want a note in the commit message, some in the methods. Use what yours agrees on.
Let the evidence speak. Tests, checks and your ability to explain every line show the work is yours.
Ask. A lead or a journal editor can tell you what they expect.
Check the venue. A journal or conference may have a disclosure policy. Read its own page before you submit.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
Goal: you will let an agent draft the documentation of its work, check each draft against ground truth and supply the reasons yourself.
Before you start: Ground Truth. Ground truth is a check the agent did not write, such as the diff or a run. A diff is the list of lines a change added and removed. A commit is a saved snapshot of your project, and git is the version control tool that keeps them.
Time: about 20 minutes.
“I do not understand what it did” is a fair worry. A paper trail answers it: short documents that say what changed, why and how to run it. The habit is to let the agent draft them, check each one against ground truth and own the why.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
The routine
Every document in this lesson follows the same four steps:

Ask. Request the draft, and say what it must cover.
Check against ground truth. Compare the draft with the real thing: the diff, a run on a clean copy, the code, the logs. Look for what the draft omits and for claims the real thing lacks.
Explain back. Say in your own words, one sentence per point, what the document records. A point you cannot put into a sentence is a point to question or leave out.
Keep, edit or revert. Decide after steps 2 and 3.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
1. Changelog
A changelog here is the agent’s short account of a change: files touched, behaviour change, what it left alone, and how to verify. The diff is the ground truth. A changelog can miss a change or overstate one, so it works as a map for reading the diff.
Ask for one after the agent finishes:
Write a changelog for the change you just made.
List the files you touched, what behaviour changed and why,
what you deliberately left alone, and one command I can run to verify it.
Mention every change in the diff, including defaults and thresholds.
Say which tests you added or ran, or say that you added none.
To check it, run git diff (changes to tracked files that you have not staged), git diff --staged (changes you have staged), or git diff --stat for a one-line-per-file summary. For a change the agent already committed, run git log -p. Run git status to list new files, which git diff does not show.

Try it on a small change
An agent was asked to fix a GC-content filter that crashed on empty sequences. This is the diff of the one file it changed (mock code):
--- a/gc_filter.py
+++ b/gc_filter.py
@@ -1,11 +1,11 @@
-MIN_GC = 40.0
+MIN_GC = 45.0
 
 
 def gc_content(seq):
-    seq = seq.strip()
+    seq = seq.strip().upper()
     gc = sum(1 for b in seq if b in "GC")
     return 100.0 * gc / len(seq)
 
 
 def keep(records):
-    return [r for r in records if gc_content(r[1]) >= MIN_GC]
+    return [r for r in records if len(r[1].strip()) > 0 and gc_content(r[1]) >= MIN_GC]
This is the agent’s changelog:
Changelog
- Files: gc_filter.py only.
- Lowercase bases now count towards GC (gc_content uppercases the sequence).
- keep() skips empty sequences instead of dividing by zero.
- Added tests for both fixes.
- Left alone: the FASTA reading code and the output format.
- Verify: python -c "from gc_filter import keep; print(keep([('a', ''), ('b', 'ggcc')]))"
Read the diff against the changelog, line by line. Two things do not match, and one of them changes which records survive the filter. Find both before you read on.
You should have found:

Omitted: MIN_GC moved from 40.0 to 45.0. Fewer records pass the filter now, and the changelog never says so.
Overstated: “Added tests for both fixes”. The diff touches one file and adds no test.

Your explain-back could be three sentences: “Lowercase bases now count. Empty sequences are skipped. The cut-off rose from 40 to 45, which I have to decide whether to keep.” Then ask the agent about the threshold, and either revert that line or keep it on purpose.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
2. ADR: the decision record
An ADR (architecture decision record) is a short note about one decision. A common layout has four parts (Nygard’s original post adds a title and a status such as proposed or accepted):

Context: the forces at play, in neutral words.
Decision: what you will do, in full sentences.
Alternatives considered: the options you weighed.
Consequences: what follows, the good and the bad.

The agent does not know your constraints: your cluster’s rules, your team’s skills, your deadline. So the decision and the reasons are yours. The agent can structure the note and draft the options. Check that every alternative is real and every consequence is listed, including the costs.
A mock example:
ADR 3: Keep the FASTA filter as a script
Status: accepted
Context: we filter reads by GC content once per project. The pipeline
  has no other Python step. Two people maintain it, both new to Nextflow.
Decision: we will keep filter_gc.py as a plain script and call it from
  the run script. We will not add a workflow step.
Alternatives considered: a workflow process (reproducible, but new machinery for
  two maintainers); a one-off notebook (no record of parameters).
Consequences: simple to read and run. Resume and containers do not
  cover this step. We revisit if a second filter appears.
Only you can say whether “two maintainers new to Nextflow” is true. Only you can confirm that line, so an agent’s draft of it is a guess to check.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
3. Commit message
Your explain-back from step 3 of the routine makes a good commit message. Use one sentence per change as the body, and the reason for a change travels with the code.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
4. README and how-to-run notes
A README records how to set up and run the project. The agent drafts it well from the files. The ground truth is a run: copy the project into an empty folder (or clone it) and type the commands exactly as written. A step that fails, or that relies on a file only your machine has, is a gap in the document.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
5. Comments and docstrings
A comment records the why that the code cannot show. Ask the agent to draft docstrings, then read each one against the code. A docstring that says “returns the GC percentage” while the function returns a fraction is wrong, and a reader will trust it.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
6. Analysis log and methods note
For science work, the log records what was run: the tools and their versions, the model and version that helped, the parameters, the input files, and what the agent did. The agent can draft it from the session. Check it against the real logs, the outputs and the output of each tool’s version command (often --version; run --help to see yours). Whatever you publish carries your name, so each line has to be right.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
section: The same habit for the next session
text:
The same habit for the next session
A handoff note records where the work stands for whoever starts next, including a fresh agent session. The routine is the same: let the agent draft it, check it against the files and git state, and edit it before you rely on it.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
When to use the habit

Small diffs: always. It costs a minute.
Large diffs: ask for a changelog per commit, so each one covers a piece you can read.
Better still: ask for work in small steps, so every diff stays small.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
Battle: the paper trail




After the next real change an agent makes for you, ask for a changelog and check it against git diff. Write down one thing it missed or overstated, or note that it matched.


Run your project’s README commands in an empty folder, exactly as written. Fix the first step that fails.

title: Should You Fine-Tune?
text:
Goal: you will say what LoRA fine-tuning is, check four conditions for it, and decide whether a task is a candidate.
Before you start: Three Kinds of Machine and Pick Your Companion.
Time: about 15 minutes. It is reading and a paper exercise; no model is trained.
A model out of the box is general. Fine-tuning trains it further on your own examples so that it handles one kind of task better. It is a heavy step with its own upkeep, so it is worth asking whether you need it. Using it is optional.

title: Should You Fine-Tune?
text:
1. What fine-tuning and LoRA are
To fine-tune a model is to continue training it on examples from your task. Its weights (the numbers it learned) change, so the result is a model of its own.
LoRA (low-rank adaptation) is one way to fine-tune. It works in three steps:

Freeze: the model’s original weights stay as they are.
Train a small adapter: you train small extra matrices (the “adapter”) on your examples.
Merge later: the adapter can be merged into the base model afterwards.

Training only the adapter needs far less memory than retraining everything.

title: Should You Fine-Tune?
text:
2. Four conditions
Consider LoRA when all of these hold:

You have the model weights. An open-weight model you can download qualifies; a hosted model reached through an API usually does not.
The task is narrow and repeatable. The same kind of input and output every time, such as tagging text with a fixed label set.
You have examples with known answers. You need enough to train on, and some held back for testing.
You have an eval. It shows that the tuned model beats the untuned one on that task.

If one condition fails, try something else first.

title: Should You Fine-Tune?
section: 3. What to try first for agent work
text:
3. What to try first for agent work
Try these in order: first a working eval, because it shows whether anything helps; then a clearer prompt, which is the cheapest thing to change; then better tools. Fine-tune last, when you can show that those fall short on a narrow task.

title: Should You Fine-Tune?
text:
4. What fine-tuning adds to track

The training data: which examples went in, and which were held back.
The adapter version: each training run gives a new one.
The base model: an adapter belongs to the base model it was trained on.

The result is a trained model that does one task, so you check it the way you check any trained model: against held-back examples on that task.

title: Should You Fine-Tune?
text:
5. Worked decision: two mock tasks
A lab keeps free-text sequencing notes. Two jobs come up.









Task A
Task B




Job
Replace sample IDs in notes with [ID]
Summarise the methods section of papers


Input
Short free-text notes
Long papers of every kind


Right answer
Clear: an ID is masked or it is not
Many acceptable summaries


Examples with known answers
2,000 notes marked by hand
A few summaries



Task A is the LoRA candidate:

It is narrow and repeatable.
It has hand-marked examples, each with a clear answer, so some can be held back.
An eval is easy to write: count IDs left in the output.

Task B has no single right answer and few examples, so a clear prompt and a check by a reader come first. If the ID pattern is fixed and known, a script handles Task A without any training.
Now pick a task from your own work and write the four conditions beside it. Mark each one yes, no or unknown. Any “no” or “unknown” is where you start.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
Goal: you will set the model and the effort on purpose, including for a subagent, and compare two settings on your own task.
Before you start: Recruit the Beast. Adopt the Pet helps with the OpenCode tab.
Time: about 15 minutes. The exercise is a worksheet and needs no model.
The companions in the Kennel are models. The harness is the program that runs a model and its tools. This page covers which companion to bring to which job, and how hard to make it think. Model names, aliases and defaults change often, so check your own tool for the current ones.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
Words to know

Model tier: a size class of model. A smaller one is faster and cheaper; a larger one is more capable and costs more.
Alias: a short nickname (such as sonnet) that the tool maps to a concrete model version.
Effort: how much the model thinks before each step.
Subagent: a helper the main agent starts with its own fresh context. It does a side task and returns only a summary. To delegate is to hand it a task.
Token: a chunk of text, the unit that usage and cost are counted in.
Context: the text the model can see right now.
Frontmatter: the small settings block at the top of a Markdown file.
Pin: name one exact model version so it never silently changes.
Inherit: use whatever the parent is using.
Prompt cache: a short-term store that makes re-reading an unchanged conversation cheaper.
Compacting: replacing the conversation history with a short summary.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
1. Two dials

Model: what the companion knows and can do.
Effort: how much it thinks per step. Lower effort means fewer and terser tool calls (the actions the agent takes, such as reading a file or running a command); higher effort means more thoroughness.

Tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
2. How to set them

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Model. The aliases are default (clears an override and names no model), best (same as opus), fable, sonnet, opus, haiku, sonnet[1m], opus[1m] (the [1m] forms ask for a longer context window), and opusplan (opus in plan mode, then sonnet for the execution). Plan mode is a mode in which the agent proposes a plan and edits nothing until you approve it. On the Anthropic API, opus, sonnet and haiku map to the current 5.5 versions; other providers can resolve the same alias to older versions.








Way
How
Note




In a session
/model <alias or name>
alone, it opens a picker; Enter saves it as your default, s keeps it for this session only


Per launch
claude --model <alias or name>



Environment
ANTHROPIC_MODEL



Settings file
model field




For results that must be reproducible (a lab pipeline, course material), pin a full model name such as claude-opus-5-5, because an alias moves when a new version ships. The variables ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL and ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL pin what each alias means.
Effort. Set it with /effort, claude --effort, the environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL, or the effortLevel setting. The levels are low, medium, high, xhigh and max, and which ones exist depends on the model. The default differs by model and by surface: for Sonnet 5.5 it is medium in Claude Code and high on the API. Run /effort in your own tool to read yours.
Per skill and per subagent. Skill files and subagent files both take model and effort in their frontmatter.

Skill: model takes the same values as /model, or inherit. A skill’s model and effort apply for the rest of that one turn and are not saved. Its effort overrides the session level but not CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL.
Subagent: model takes sonnet, opus, haiku, fable, a full model ID, or inherit. effort takes low to max. If the subagent’s model differs from the main one and you give no effort, the session level does not apply to it, so set it.
Which model a subagent gets, first match wins: the per-call model parameter, then the definition’s model, then the environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL, then the main conversation’s model.

A subagent is a Markdown file with frontmatter in .claude/agents/ (project) or ~/.claude/agents/ (yours):
---
name: log-reader
description: Reads long pipeline logs and reports only failed tasks with their error lines.
model: haiku
effort: medium
---
Read the logs you are given. Return: task name, exit status, the first error line.
Quote lines exactly. If something is unclear, say so.
A tools field can also limit what the helper may use. The sub-agents page in Lore has the exact syntax.
This sketch uses medium because Haiku 5.5 at low is more likely to skip a search, stop early or skip a check. For reading logs, catching every failure is the point.



/models picks a model for the current session only; the config file is unchanged.
opencode run --model provider/model-id sets it for one run. The format is provider/model-id, with an optional #variant such as #high. IDs are case-sensitive.
The model key in opencode.json (or opencode.jsonc) sets your default.
An agent can have its own model key. A subagent with no model inherits the parent session’s model. The frontmatter example is mode: subagent plus model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5#high.
A local Ollama model is selectable like any other, for example ollama/gemma3:4b.

Haiku: fastest replies and lowest cost; suited to subagent tasks.
Sonnet: everyday coding and agent work.
Opus: complex agentic coding; most workloads start here.
Fable: the hardest, long-running work.

title: Pick Your Companion
section: 4. When the output is not good enough: the upgrade ladder
text:
4. When the output is not good enough: the upgrade ladder
Climb one rung at a time and re-check after each.

Add a way to verify. A test, a script, a count against an independent tool, a second look that does not share the first one’s blind spot. Without it you cannot tell whether the next rungs helped.
Raise effort one level.
Change the model to the next tier up.

Cheap-then-retry: if outcomes are checkable (tests, or a verifier, which is a separate check that tests the output), run at low effort and re-run only the failures at higher effort. A checker that passes bad work lets failures through, and a failure costs two runs of waiting time.
Compare cost per finished task, because failed tasks still cost money and a few hard tasks can carry much of the bill.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
5. Delegation hygiene

Keep the expensive model’s context lean. Sending bulk reading to a subagent keeps that reading out of the main conversation.
Spot-check summaries. A subagent returns only a summary, and summaries omit and distort. Ask for exact quotes or file paths and open two yourself. Many subagents returning long answers can also fill the main context again.
State your rules in the delegation prompt. The built-in Explore subagent (a read-only search helper) and Plan subagent (a read-only research helper used in plan mode) skip CLAUDE.md, the instructions file the tool loads at session start. A rule like “never touch raw/” must be written into the task you hand them. Custom subagents load CLAUDE.md unless set to skip it.
Switch models at a quiet moment. Switching model mid-conversation can change prompt-cache behaviour, and the tool may ask you to confirm.
Change effort between sessions when you are comparing. Changing top-level effort mid-session also invalidates the cache.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
6. Measure on your own task
Pick one small real task that has an outcome check (a test that passes, a count that matches).

Choose two settings to compare, for example the same model at medium and high. Change only one thing.
For each, start a fresh session, run the task three times, and record pass or fail from the outcome check.
After each run, open /usage and note the “Usage by model” block. The dollar figure is an estimate computed locally at list price, and on a subscription you may see plan usage bars instead. /usage resets on /clear.
Compare cost per passing run. Three runs is a small sample: it can expose a big difference, and a small one needs more runs.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
7. What you gave up
Choosing wrongly costs you in both directions. Too small or too low: the companion loses the thread, skips checks or stops early, and you redo the work, often after you have already trusted it. Too big or too high: the same job costs more and runs slower, and you may not notice because the answer looks fine. The checks above are how you notice either mistake.

title: Pick Your Companion
text:
8. Other model families
The ideas above carry over to other families; the names do not. Mistral is one example:

Models: Ministral 3 comes in 3B, 8B and 14B, and Mistral Small 4 is also open-weight; both are Apache 2.0. Check Mistral’s models page for current names and deprecation dates.
Harness: Mistral Vibe is an open-source terminal coding agent (Apache 2.0) with four approval modes. Its config file is ~/.vibe/config.toml.

ask: asks before any tool.
accept-edits: the default; applies file edits without asking, and still asks before shell commands.
smart-approve: see the Vibe docs for how it decides.
auto-approve: for trusted, sandboxed environments only.

Trusted folders: Vibe loads project config only from folders you have trusted. Start in ask until you trust the project.
Local models: Vibe works with any model served behind an OpenAI-compatible API, such as vLLM, llama.cpp, LM Studio or Ollama. Check the Vibe docs for the Ollama setup.

When you switch families, redo the worksheet below. A tier ladder built on one vendor’s models does not carry over name for name.

text:
Exercise: assign six jobs
No model needed. For each mock job, write down a model (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus or Fable), an effort (low, medium, high) and whether you would use a subagent, then open the key.

Rename 200 sample IDs in a samplesheet to a new scheme, given a mapping table.
Summarise the methods section of one paper into five bullets for your lab notes.
Debug a Nextflow stage that fails on one sample and passes on the others.
Classify 5,000 free-text tissue labels into 12 categories, with 200 hand-tagged rows to check against.

Answer key (several answers are defensible)


Probably no model at all. A mapping table and a script do this exactly, and a script cannot invent an ID. If you use a model, Haiku at low or medium, with a diff or count check; no subagent needed.
Sonnet, medium, no subagent. The text is short, so there is no context to protect. Check two claims against the paper yourself.
Sonnet at medium, raised to high or Opus if the first attempt fails and a test says so. Keep it in the main conversation, because the debugging needs the history. Add a failing test first (rung 1).

Opus, high, in plan mode, main conversation. A weak plan is expensive downstream and other people depend on the script. Ask for a test plan too.
Sonnet, low or medium, no subagent. It is a short, checkable question: try the suggested fix. Escalate when the explanation does not hold up.



Check what model and effort your tool is using right now (/model, /effort) and write them down.


Run the same small task at two settings and compare the result and /usage.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
Goal: you will say what a cloud session is, what leaves your machine when you start one, which jobs suit it, and how to review what comes back.
Before you start: Recruit the Beast and The Locked Cabinet. You need git and a GitHub account only if you later start a session.
Time: about 15 minutes. The exercise is a worksheet on a mock file tree and needs no cloud account or model.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
The rule for this page






NoteCloud sessions are for drafting scripts and documentation. Data analysis stays on your machine or the cluster.



Use a cloud session for writing scripts, updating documentation and similar low-risk text work. Real data, controlled data, sample sheets with identifiers, genotypes and results stay out of a cloud session and its repository. Analysis runs on your own machine or the cluster, under your data agreement.
Think of the cloud agent as a drafting helper that returns a branch (a named line of commits in git) which you review and then run yourself, where the data lives.


Cloud sessions are optional. If you use one, the rest of the page shows how to keep sensitive material at home.

title: Claude in the Cloud
Claude in the Cloud
text:
2. What leaves your machine
Read this part twice. When you start a cloud session:

Your repository contents are cloned onto Anthropic’s VM. Anthropic reads only the repository you start the session in.
Your prompts and everything the agent reads and writes go to the model.
The session transcript (the saved record of the whole conversation, including tool output) is stored by Anthropic so you can return to it later.
Retention (how long Anthropic keeps stored data) follows your account type. Consumer plans keep it 5 years if you allow training and 30 days if you do not. Commercial plans (Team, Enterprise, API) keep it 30 days as standard. Check your own plan for its current terms. Deleting a cloud session permanently removes its event data.
All outbound traffic from Anthropic-hosted sessions passes through a proxy (a go-between server that forwards requests, here for audit logging and abuse prevention).
Network level None may still let data exit. A network access level is the setting that says which internet hosts the VM may reach (None, Limited or Full; see section 5). The Anthropic API stays reachable even at None, which may allow data to exit the VM.
Environment variables (named settings handed to programs, often used for keys) set in a cloud environment can be read by any command Claude runs, and anyone who uses that environment can read the values.
Sharing: a session can be visible to others, and sessions may contain code and credentials from private repositories.

Three organisation settings block cloud sessions outright: Zero Data Retention, a HIPAA configuration (HIPAA is the US health-data privacy law) and customer-managed encryption keys (your organisation holds the keys). If your organisation uses one of them, cloud sessions are not available. Your administrator can also switch cloud sessions off (the allow_remote_sessions policy).
Keep controlled data out of the cloud repository. Treat the clone, the transcript and anything you paste as held by Anthropic. Read your data agreement before you push anything to a remote that a cloud session can see (a remote is the copy of a repository hosted elsewhere, such as on GitHub).

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
3. Good uses and bad uses







Fine for a cloud session (code and mock data only)
Keep for your machine or the cluster




Write a samplesheet validator, tested on a three-row mock file
Run the analysis


Write a QC summary plotting script, developed on mock data
Load real counts, genotypes or results


Draft or update the README, changelog, docstrings
Debug with real sample IDs in the repository


Refactor non-data code that has tests
Anything under a data agreement


Review a pull request that holds no identifiers
Anything that needs a local database or the cluster


Triage issues that hold no identifiers
Anything that needs your institution’s network or files



A session has a roughly 30 GB disk and no GPU is listed. Work that needs a GPU, a VPN or local databases stays on your side.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
4. How to start

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama



Push first. claude --cloud "your task" starts a cloud session from your terminal. It clones the GitHub remote at your current branch, and your local folder is not used. Commit and push (save snapshots, then upload them to the remote) before you start, so the session sees your latest work. If the branch is not on GitHub the CLI prints Branch <name> is not on GitHub, and the session starts from a pushed commit or the default branch. One repository per session. You can also start from claude.ai/code in the browser.
Write a ticket-style prompt. That is a self-contained note like a work ticket: the problem, the expected result, and a command that proves it (in the example, pytest, a Python test runner). Be specific, name files and paste errors. Example, with no data in it:

Problem: scripts/validate_samplesheet.py accepts duplicate sample IDs.
Expected: exit status 1 and a message naming the duplicated ID.
Check: pytest tests/test_validate_samplesheet.py (mock rows only).
Add a test for the duplicate case. Only change files under scripts/ and tests/.
A repository with no data/ or results/ folders is the safe one. A prompt line such as “do not read data/” is a request to the model and gives no protection. If the folder is in the repository, the cloud session can read it.

If there is no remote. When a repository has no GitHub remote, or the Claude GitHub App (a program you install on a repository or organisation to grant it limited access) is not on it, Claude Code bundles the repository and uploads it: full history of all branches plus uncommitted changes to tracked files, under 100 MB. Untracked files are left out. On macOS, Linux and WSL the upload needs git 2.31 or later; with an older git the CLI refuses to start the session and tells you to update. On those systems, uncommitted changes to .env, *.pem, *.tfvars, id_rsa and Git LFS-managed files (large files stored outside normal git history) are skipped; on native Windows everything tracked uploads. Keep data out of this route entirely. Your history may already hold a file you deleted, and the bundle takes all of it. Check what is tracked and what your .gitignore covers first. Non-GitHub hosts can only use the bundle, and cannot push back.
/web-setup, typed inside Claude Code (not in your shell), sends your gh auth token (GitHub’s command-line login token) to Anthropic so cloud sessions can reach your repositories without the GitHub App. It needs a claude.ai sign-in; API-key sign-in does not work, and neither does a Bedrock or Vertex-style provider. On Team and Enterprise plans an Owner has to enable it first.
Getting the session back: teleport. To teleport is to pull a cloud session into your local terminal: claude --teleport (shows a picker), claude --teleport <session-id>, or /teleport (alias /tp) inside a session. It needs a clean git state (it offers to stash your changes, that is, set them aside temporarily with git stash), the same repository (not a fork, which is your own copy of someone else’s repository), the branch pushed, and the same claude.ai account.
GitHub access, in short. Two ways in: the GitHub App or your /web-setup token. For Anthropic-hosted sessions, your GitHub credential is stored encrypted on Anthropic’s servers and does not enter the VM; the VM holds a short-lived credential, and a GitHub proxy swaps it in. The proxy rejects branch deletions and tag pushes, but it does not limit which branches a push can update. Use GitHub branch protection or rulesets (rules on which branches may be changed and by whom) for that. A rule that the connected access can bypass will not block the push.



To run an agent away from your laptop with OpenCode, run it yourself in your own container or virtual machine. That is your own infrastructure and your own responsibility.
A local Ollama model keeps prompts on your machine, though web or tool calls the agent makes may leave it. If your data agreement rules out third-party processing, ask whether this local route is allowed.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
5. Environments
An environment is a saved configuration for cloud sessions: network access, environment variables, a setup script and network secrets. A first-time setup creates one called Default, with Limited access.
Network access levels:







Level
What the VM can reach




None
No internet (the Anthropic API, the GitHub proxy and enabled connectors still work)


Limited
A default allowlist (a list of the only hosts permitted) of package registries, GitHub and cloud SDKs, plus domains you add


Full
Any host



Pick the narrowest level that lets the task finish.

Setup scripts: a setup script is a Bash script that runs once as root before Claude starts, to install what the task needs. It must exit with status 0 and should stay under about five minutes, or it is not cached. The result is cached as a filesystem snapshot (packages and files stay; running processes and databases do not), and rebuilt when the script or allowed hosts change or after about 7 days. Installs need network access, so None blocks them.
Environment variables versus network secrets: environment variables are readable by any command Claude runs. Network secrets are the safer option where possible: the key stays outside the VM, and Anthropic’s agent proxy adds it to requests to hosts you list.
Preinstalled tools: Python with pip, uv, poetry and pytest, Node, Ruby, PHP, Java, Go, Rust, C and C++, Docker, PostgreSQL 16, Redis, git, gh and jq. No R, conda or bioinformatics tools are listed. Ask Claude to run check-tools to see what is present.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
6. Permission modes in the cloud
A permission mode says how much the agent may do before asking you. Cloud sessions offer three: Accept edits, Plan and Auto (your organisation can switch Auto off). There is no Manual and no Bypass mode in the cloud, and a bypassPermissions setting in your files is ignored there. You pick the mode in the dropdown; there is no --cloud flag for it.
Use Plan for anything you do not already understand, and read the plan before it edits. You can also plan locally with claude --permission-mode plan, commit and push the plan, and then start claude --cloud.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
7. Limits and failure modes

A fresh machine every time. An idle VM pauses and may later be reclaimed (taken back by the system). Files are kept while it is paused. Commit and push work you want to keep. Reopening restores the conversation, but running commands and subagents (helper agents the main agent started) are lost.
Timeouts. A foreground command defaults to 2 minutes (up to 10), then moves to the background for up to 30 more.
Size. Approximate ceilings are 4 vCPUs, 16 GB RAM and 30 GB disk. Heavy jobs may be stopped.
Shared usage. Cloud work counts against the same plan limits as all your other Claude Code use. Check your plan’s limits.
GitHub comments under your name. Claude can reply on pull requests under your GitHub name, marked as from Claude Code. That can trigger any comment-driven automation you have set up.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
8. Review what comes back
The result is a branch. Treat it like a stranger’s pull request: it may be fine and it may be wrong.

Read the diff (the list of changed lines) as you would any other.
Look for accidents in the diff: committed data files, absolute paths, sample IDs in a test or a comment, a .env, a notebook saved with outputs (a notebook is a Jupyter document mixing code and results; its saved outputs are the tables and plots stored inside the file).
Run the tests locally, on your machine.
Only then run the script on your data, locally or on the cluster, under your data agreement. The cloud agent never saw that data and never ran that step.

A green test in the cloud is a claim to verify. A test passing on mock data tells you the script runs; your real data is the next check, run locally.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
Exercise: the safe-to-send checklist
No cloud account and no model needed. Open tree.txt, a mock repository tree (every name is invented).

Mark each path that must not reach anything a cloud session can see. Say whether it needs removing from history (it is already committed) or only ignoring, and write one reason each.
Write the .gitignore lines that would have stopped it.
Draft a ticket-style prompt for one low-risk task: update docs/usage.md, or add a missing-column test to scripts/validate_samplesheet.py. Include the problem, the expected result and a check that uses only data/mock/.



Answer key (some entries depend on your data agreement)

Every listed path below is in the tree as committed, so each one needs removing from history before you push anything a cloud session can see. The ignore lines further down only prevent a repeat.
Paths to remove:

.env: a secret. It was already committed, so remove it from history and replace the token; ignoring it helps only from now on.
samplesheet_real.csv: identifiers and genotype calls.
data/raw/ and data/processed/: real reads and real counts.
notebooks/01_qc.ipynb and notebooks/02_diffexp.ipynb: outputs saved inside them contain real sample IDs, tables and plots. Clear the outputs, or keep the notebooks out.
results/ (including de_genes.csv and pca_real_samples.png): results.
logs/slurm-482913.out: real sample IDs and cluster paths.
notebooks/.ipynb_checkpoints/: autosave copies of the notebooks, with the same saved outputs.

Fine to send (they hold no real data): README.md, environment.yml, samplesheet_template.csv, config/params.yaml (check it for real paths), data/mock/, docs/, scripts/, tests/.
Ignore lines that would help:
.env
.env.*
samplesheet_real.csv
*.fastq.gz
data/raw/
data/processed/
results/
logs/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
Add a rule for notebooks too (for example, a pre-commit hook, a script git runs automatically before each commit, that clears outputs), because .gitignore alone cannot strip outputs from a notebook you do want to commit. Likewise, .gitignore only stops files that are not yet tracked; anything already committed stays in history until you remove it properly, and rewriting history is its own careful job.
Sample prompt:
Problem: docs/usage.md does not mention the --strandedness option added in v0.3.
Expected: a short section with the option, its allowed values, and one example
command using data/mock/ only.
Check: the example command in the new section runs on data/mock/counts_mock.tsv. Only edit docs/usage.md.
A prompt line is a request to the model. The safe version of this repository has no real data folders to read.

title: Claude in the Cloud

What to remember

Cloud sessions are for drafting scripts and documentation; analysis stays on your machine or the cluster. Real data, controlled data, sample sheets with identifiers, genotypes and results stay out of a cloud session and its repository.
Your repository contents, prompts and session transcript go to Anthropic, and network level None may still let data exit the VM.
Return is a branch: read the diff, look for stray data, run the tests locally, then run on your data where it lives, under your data agreement.

title: Plug In a Server
text:
Goal: you will treat an MCP server as software you install, then scope it, limit it and read what it sends back.
Before you start: Grow the Carapace. A permission rule allows, asks about or denies a tool call. The sandbox is an operating-system layer that limits what shell commands can touch.
Time: about 15 minutes.
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems. A server is the piece on the other side: it offers the harness tools or data, such as an issue tracker, a database or a monitoring system. MCP is optional. It widens what the agent can reach, and every widening is a decision.

title: Plug In a Server
section: A server is software you installed
text:
A server is software you installed
A stdio server (a program the harness starts locally and talks to over its input/output) is a command that Claude Code launches on your machine (claude mcp add ... -- <command>), and secrets can be passed to it as environment variables. Assume it can do whatever that command can do with the credentials you gave it.
Verify you trust each server before connecting it. Servers that fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection: text from a file, web page or tool that the model treats as an instruction.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Add a remote server over HTTP (the transport: how the harness talks to the server; an http server is remote), and a local one (everything after -- is passed to the server untouched):
claude mcp add --transport http mydocs https://example.com/mcp
claude mcp add --env API_KEY=your-key-here myserver -- <command> [args...]
Run claude mcp add --help for the current flags. Inside a session, /mcp lists the servers and their tools. An older transport called SSE (server-sent events, one-way streaming over HTTP) is deprecated in favour of HTTP where a server offers both.
Three scopes (who or where a setting applies) decide who gets the server (set with -s/--scope):







Scope
Where it applies




Local (the default)
this project only, for you alone; stored in ~/.claude.json


Project
everyone on the project, via .mcp.json in the project root


User
all your projects; stored in ~/.claude.json



A project-scoped server is a file in the repository:
{ "mcpServers": { "shared-server": { "type": "http", "url": "https://example.com/mcp" } } }
In interactive sessions, Claude Code asks for approval before using project-scoped servers from .mcp.json. claude mcp reset-project-choices resets your answers. Read that file as you would read a script from a stranger’s repository, because it asks to start something on your machine.
In claude -p and Agent SDK (software development kit) runs, which are headless (non-interactive), there is no prompt and project-scoped servers load without asking. --strict-mcp-config is one mitigation.
Each server’s tools appear in permission rules as mcp__<server>__<tool>, and mcp__<server>__* (a matcher, a pattern that selects names) matches every tool of one server. Tool definitions are deferred (loaded only when needed) by default, so only tool names and server instructions take up context until a tool is used.


In the V2 docs, servers go under mcp.servers; V2 does not put server names directly under mcp. Check which version you have installed. A remote server:
{ "mcp": { "servers": { "mydocs": {
    "type": "remote",
    "url": "https://example.com/mcp",
    "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {env:MCP_API_KEY}" } } } } }
A local one uses "type": "local" and a command array. Set "disabled": true to switch a server off. MCP tools consume model context, so add only the servers you need.
Permissions are an ordered array where the last match wins and no match means ask. An MCP tool’s action is <server>_<tool> with resource *. Check the current docs for whether OpenCode asks before using a project-level server.

title: Plug In a Server
section: What comes back is text to read
text:
What comes back is text to read
A server that fetches web pages, tickets or messages hands text written by someone else to the model. That text can contain sentences aimed at the agent (“ignore the above and …”), and the model may follow them. Habits that limit the damage:

Prefer read-only servers and read-only credentials. A server that cannot write cannot be talked into writing.
Give least privilege, only the access the job needs: one project, one scope, a token limited to what you need.
Read before adding: who publishes it, what tools it lists, what it asks for. Unneeded servers are also unneeded context.
Read fetched content sceptically, and supervise any write access an agent uses on it.
Deny the dangerous tools by name. Permission rules still apply to server tools.

The sandbox limits shell commands even if a prompt injection bypasses the model’s decision-making. A server can take other routes, so treat the sandbox as one layer.

title: Plug In a Server
text:
Where a server comes from
Servers, skills and plugins either run code or supply instructions to the agent, so each is a way in. A listing in a registry means the thing is easy to find. The official MCP registry lists self-reported data and runs no security review.

Prefer a source that records the maintainer and a review date.
Check what the interface is allowed to do before you connect it.
Ask your institution for a vetted list. If it has none, treat every interface as unvetted.
Hidden instructions are possible. A tool description can carry instructions you never see, and a skill’s instructions can tell the agent to send results to an outside address.


Pick an MCP server you might use. Write down who publishes it, the tools it lists, the credential it needs, and whether a read-only version exists. Hold off installing it for now.

title: Advice or Enforcement
text:

Before you start: Guard the Door. A sandbox is an operating-system layer that limits what shell commands can touch.
Time: about 15 minutes.
Every control does one of three things.
The rule of thumb: advice for preferences, a prompt for decisions you want to make each time, enforcement for things that must never happen.

A hook that exits 0 with no JSON decision adds no control: it expresses no decision and the normal permission flow runs. (A hook can also exit 0 and print a JSON deny decision, which does block.) Deny and ask rules are still evaluated when a hook returns allow. The sandbox’s restrictions still apply if a prompt injection bypasses the model’s decision.

Enforces

Enforces when it denies
Runs only for allow and ask.


Git history

title: Advice or Enforcement
text:
Limits for research groups
The same split works for a group that runs agents:

Put limits in the system that runs the agent: permission scopes, and spend caps in the metering system (the system that counts usage and cost). A budget the agent can exceed is not a limit.
Name a human owner for each agent duty.
Log what an agent did under an identity you can trace.
Keep a list of the agents in use, including personal ones connected to mail or files. Institutions can keep one, and a group can keep its own.
Use a scoped account, take a backup before granting write or delete access, and name an owner for the machine. An over-privileged agent with shell access can wipe data on a shared lab server.

title: The Project Charter
text:
Goal: you will give the agent standing instructions for a project, and know where instructions end and enforcement begins.
Before you start: Write the Brief. Who Said What helps.
Time: about 15 minutes.
Typing the same background every session is wasteful. A project instructions file is read at the start so the agent already knows the project’s conventions.

title: The Project Charter
text:
What goes in
Put in facts the agent cannot guess: how to run the tests, where data lives, naming conventions, “never edit raw/”. Keep it short (aim for under 200 lines per file) because very long instructions are followed less well.
Write the file yourself first and read what /init produces critically. A generated file can contain wrong guesses about your project.

title: The Project Charter
text:
Where instructions end
Instructions are advice. The instructions file is loaded as context, and a line saying “never delete files” cannot stop a delete. Enforcement comes from permission rules (rules that allow, ask or deny a tool call), hooks (scripts that run before or after a tool call), and managed settings (organisation-set rules you cannot override).

title: The Project Charter
text:
Keep the file current
Instruction files go stale: a rule written for an older model, a path that no longer exists, two files that disagree. When instructions contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily.
In Claude Code (v2.1.283 or later), /doctor prompt-audit checks your instruction files for outdated or conflicting content and writes a report with proposed edits. (/doctor is a bundled skill, a ready-made skill that ships inside the tool.) It changes nothing until you ask, and it checks content only, so size and cost are out of scope. The audit is itself a model reading your files, so review its suggestions like any other output. In OpenCode, review the file by hand.

title: The Project Charter
section: Write docs for the agent too
text:
Write docs for the agent too
An agent works on your code and data from the docstrings and descriptions it finds. Write them as if an agent will re-run the work:

Units, data versions and assumptions: put them in the docstring or next to the code.
Renames: update the docstring when you rename a parameter. An agent that reads an old docstring calls a name that no longer exists.
Stale documentation: it leads to results that look plausible and are wrong.


Write a short instructions file (about ten lines) for one of your real projects: how to run its tests, where data lives, and one thing the agent should leave alone.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
Goal: you will ask an agent for a plan before it edits, review that plan like a reviewer, and know what a plan can and cannot guarantee.
Before you start: Write the Brief. The exercise uses mock files on your laptop and runs no model.
Time: about 20 minutes.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
Why plan first
A wrong plan costs you a paragraph to read and reject. A wrong 400-line diff (the list of lines a change added and removed) costs you the time to review it, and the longer it is, the more likely you approve something you did not understand. A plan is the cheapest piece to ask for first. Ask for small pieces, and accept only as much output as you can honestly review.
Use plan mode for changes you want to review before they touch disk.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
How: plan mode
Words used below:

Session: one conversation with the agent.
Shell commands: commands you would type in a terminal, such as ls or git status.
Context: everything the model can see in the session.
Subagent: a helper with its own context window; only its summary comes back.
Deny rule: a rule that blocks an action in every mode.
Auto mode: a mode where a background check decides what runs without a prompt.
Bypass permissions: a startup option (--dangerously-skip-permissions) that turns most prompts off.
-p: runs one command with no chat (non-interactive mode).
Agent SDK: a library for building your own agent programs.


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


In Claude Code, plan mode is a permission mode: a setting for what the agent may do without asking you. In plan mode the agent reads files, may run shell commands to explore, and writes a plan. It is meant to leave your source files unedited until you approve the plan (tell it to go ahead).
Three ways in:

Shift+Tab during a session, until the status bar shows ⏸ plan mode on.
/plan followed by your request, for example /plan add a strandedness column to the samplesheet parser.
claude --permission-mode plan when you start it.

When the plan is ready, the agent presents it and asks how to proceed. The options, with their exact labels:

Yes, and use auto mode: auto mode decides what runs without a prompt. If auto mode is unavailable, this reads Yes, auto-accept edits. If your session started with bypass, it reads Yes, and switch to BYPASS PERMISSIONS (no further prompts) for this session. Bypass skips most prompts.
Yes, manually approve edits: each edit still asks you.
No, keep planning: you say what to change.

The setting showClearContextOnPlanAccept adds a first option that approves and also clears the planning context. Look at your approval prompt to see whether it is on.






Note



At the approval prompt, Shift+Tab approves the plan. If you want to think, change something or back out, press Esc first. To leave plan mode when no prompt is open, press Shift+Tab.


Two more details:

Where the plan lives: plans are written to ~/.claude/plans/ by default (the plansDirectory setting changes the folder). Ctrl+G opens the proposed plan in your default text editor so you can edit it before the agent proceeds. Approving exits plan mode and switches to the mode you chose; to plan again, use Shift+Tab or /plan.
Side helper: in plan mode the agent can hand research to the built-in Plan subagent. It is read-only, so the main conversation stays read-only too.



OpenCode has a built-in plan agent. It explores and plans without editing normal project files, and it can edit only under its plan directory, ~/.opencode/plan. That edit restriction is a deny rule, and saved approvals do not override a deny. Its shell commands follow the normal permission rules.
The base policy for every agent allows everything except asking before reading .env files, so shell commands can run without a prompt. Check the permission rules in your version before you rely on the plan agent.
You can turn the plan agent off with {"agents": {"plan": {"disabled": true}}}.
To find out how to switch to the plan agent and whether it has an approval step, read the OpenCode agents page for your version.

title: Plan Before You Edit
section: Review the plan like a reviewer
text:
Review the plan like a reviewer
A plan is text from a model that has not yet run anything. Read it the way you would read a methods section from a collaborator you have not worked with before. A checklist:

What files will it touch? Anything outside the task is a question to ask.
What does it assume about the data? “IDs are unique” or “the file has a header” are guesses until checked against the real files.
What could it break? Callers, config, tests, outputs other people read.
How will it verify, and is the check independent of the code it writes? A test the agent writes for its own code can share its mistake. Compute one value some other way, for example with awk or wc.
Are the steps small enough to review one at a time? A step names one change, so “Update everything” needs splitting.
What is not in the plan? Missing edge cases, missing tests, no mention of a rollback.

If an answer is bad, choose No, keep planning and say what to change, or edit the plan yourself with Ctrl+G.

title: Plan Before You Edit
section: What a plan does not guarantee
text:
What a plan does not guarantee

A plan is advice. An approved plan is only as good as your review of it.
The agent can deviate. The agent can still change course after approval. Afterwards, read the diff against the plan: every changed file should be one the plan named. /code-review reviews the diff in a fresh subagent that never saw your conversation.
Plan mode may be an instruction only. In an interactive terminal session where bypass permissions is available, Claude is only instructed to plan without editing. Claude Code does not enforce it, and edits and shell commands run without a prompt (explicit ask rules and a few critical deletions still prompt). With -p, the Agent SDK and the VS Code chat panel, the blocks stay in place.
Deny rules always apply. A deny rule blocks in every mode, plan mode included.
Read-only has gaps. Plan mode holds back edits. Test how your MCP tools and shell commands behave in it before you trust it near anything important.
The plan sits outside your repository by default. The plan file lives in ~/.claude/plans/. Keep your own project under Git.

title: Plan Before You Edit
section: When to plan, and when not to
text:
When to plan, and when not to

One-line fix with an obvious check: just ask for it.
Unfamiliar code, changes across several files, and anything that touches paths where your data lives: plan first.
Open-ended exploring: a vague prompt is fine, at the cost of more correction.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
Keep the approved plan
The plan in ~/.claude/plans/ is easy to lose track of. Ask the agent to save the approved plan into your project, for example as PLAN.md, then commit it.
A related pattern: ask the agent to interview you until it could write the spec, save it as SPEC.md, then start a fresh session (an empty conversation) to build from it. The fresh session has a clean context and a written definition of done.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
Exercise: review a bad plan
Everything here is a mock on your laptop, and no model runs. Save mock-plan.md and samplesheet.csv. The plan says it will make a samplesheet parser accept a new strandedness column. Read the CSV, then go through the six checklist questions and write down every problem you find. Aim for at least four.


Answer key


No verification step. Step 6 reports success, and no step runs the parser or compares against an independent count.
A file outside the parser. Step 4 edits conf/base.config and renames a parameter, which can break every command line and config that uses the old name. The task covered only the parser.
An unchecked assumption about the data. Step 3 says sample IDs are unique. In the CSV, S03 appears twice (lanes L1 and L2), so a dictionary keyed by sample_id silently keeps only one row.
One step is too big. Step 5 covers modules, docs and tests at once. Ask for it to be split and reviewed piece by piece.
Also worth noting: S04 has an empty fastq_2, and the plan leaves that open (what is not in the plan). Step 2’s default of unstranded may quietly hide a missing column in a real run.



Review the plan the agent proposes for your next real task with the checklist before approving. Write down one thing you changed or rejected.


Ask for the plan to be saved to a file in your project, and open the file to check it matches what you approved.

title: Close the Loop
text:
Goal: you will turn “it did the wrong thing” into a measured fix, and know when the fix has stopped working.
Before you start: Forge a Skill. A Skill is a procedure the agent loads when it is relevant.
Time: about 10 minutes.
Sooner or later the agent does something you did not want: it skips a check, names files badly, or uses a method your lab avoids. A chat correction helps that one reply, and a Skill helps next time. An eval tells you whether the fix works, and keeps telling you after the model or tool changes.

title: Close the Loop
text:
What is an eval?
An eval (short for evaluation) is a repeatable check of how well an AI system does a task. It is the AI version of a unit test, with one difference. Ordinary code gives the same output for the same input, so a test can assert one answer. A model can answer the same prompt differently each time, so you run the check several times and ask how often, and how well, it does the job.
Trying a few favourite prompts and judging whether it “feels better” is a quick start but a weak habit. A new model, a new prompt or a new Skill can help one task and hurt another, and you will not see it from a handful of tries. An eval runs the same cases every time, so a change shows up as a number you can compare.
An eval has three parts:

Cases: the prompts you test with, plus what a good answer looks like.
Task: the thing under test, here the agent with or without your Skill.
Graders: the checks that mark each answer.

Graders come in three kinds:









Kind
How it marks
Strength
Weakness




Deterministic
A script checks something exact.
Free, fast, same every time.
Covers only what a rule can state.


Human
You read the output and judge it.
Best for quality and style.
Slow, does not scale.


Judge model
A second model marks against a rubric.
Handles open-ended output at scale.
Costs a call per mark, can be wrong.



A deterministic check looks like this: the file exists, the command ran, the output has 3 columns. Use deterministic graders wherever you can, a person where you must, and a judge model for the rest. Because answers vary, the result is usually a pass rate (for example 2 of 3 runs, or 80% of graders passed) and not one pass or fail. The useful question is whether a change moved that number up or down.
The cases decide how good the eval is. A set of cases should look like your real work and include awkward ones: an empty file, a misspelt name, a request phrased differently. Ten realistic cases beat a hundred invented ones. Real failures are the best source, which is why the loop below starts with Notice.

title: Close the Loop
text:
The loop

Notice. Something did not go your way. Write down the prompt you used and what was wrong with the result.
Steer. Write or edit a Skill (or an instructions-file line) that says what to do instead. Keep it short and concrete.
Measure. Run the same prompt with the Skill and without it, several times each. Models vary between runs, so several tries give a fairer picture than one.
Compare. If with is clearly better than without, the Skill earns its place. If they are about the same, the Skill adds little: it may not be triggering, it may repeat what the model already does, or it may be too vague.
Repeat later. A new model version can make a Skill unnecessary, or break it. Re-run the evals when the model, the tool, or the Skill changes.

The number that matters is the difference between with and without. The without run is the baseline: it shows what the model does on its own. A Skill that scores 100% both ways has added nothing the model lacked.

title: Close the Loop
text:
What to check

The result: does the output have what you asked for (a file exists, a command was run, a number matches)? Prefer checks a script can do.
The process: was the Skill actually used? A good-looking answer without the Skill loading means the Skill is not the reason.
Cost: every run is a real model call. Start with few cases and few runs, and raise them only for a Skill you will rely on.

Evals can be wrong too. A check that always passes, or that fails correct answers, tells you little. Read a few raw outputs by hand before trusting a score.

title: Close the Loop
section: Four habits before you rely on a tool
text:
Four habits before you rely on a tool

Known answers: test on cases where you already know the right answer.
Repeat: run each case several times, since one pass can be luck.
Write down failures: keep a list of the failure modes you see.
Test again: repeat the tests when the tool, the model or your task changes.

When a model does the grading, a judge from the same family as the model being judged is not an independent grader. Check a sample of its marks by hand against reference answers fixed in advance.

Keep a short list of the times an agent went wrong for you. Each entry is a candidate Skill and a ready-made eval case.

title: The Locked Cabinet
text:
Goal: you will keep keys, settings and sensitive data out of the agent’s reach, and know what changes on a shared cluster.
Before you start: Grow the Carapace. A deny rule is a setting that blocks the agent’s file-reading tool from a path.
Time: about 15 minutes.
Much research data is not sensitive. Some of it is, and then special agreements apply. Your own data agreement and your cluster’s policy come first. This quest uses no real data and practises habits, so that the careful choice becomes automatic.

title: The Locked Cabinet
text:
Three ideas

A prompt may leave your machine. With a hosted model, anything the agent reads may be sent to the provider. A model running locally (on your own machine, for example through Ollama) keeps prompts on your machine, though web or tool calls it makes may not. Your agreement decides whether either is allowed for your data.
Secrets stay out of content. API keys, tokens, SSH keys and passwords belong in a secret store, kept out of the project folder, and out of chats and any instructions file you commit. An environment variable is visible to any command the agent runs, so a read rule alone does not seal it.
A shared cluster is shared. What is fine on your laptop can disturb other people on a login node, or break a data policy on shared storage. Cluster rules apply to agents exactly as they apply to you.







Note



A deny rule on your secrets files stops the agent’s file-reading tool. It does not apply to a Python or Node script that opens the file itself. So also keep secrets out of the project folder, and use a sandbox or shell rules where you can. For another tool, check its documentation on shell reads of denied files.

title: The Locked Cabinet
section: Personal data and where an agent may send it
text:
Personal data and where an agent may send it

Reading a file discloses it. With an externally hosted model, everything the agent reads goes to the provider. If the agent opens a project .env file, treat its keys as exposed and rotate them. Keep secrets outside folders the agent can read.
Personal data needs more than a no-training promise. Sending personal data to a provider can count as processing under GDPR (the EU data protection law). Ask your data steward which accounts are approved, and use an institutional account for work. Ask them too whether you need a lawful basis (a legal reason to process), a processor contract (a written agreement with the provider) and a transfer basis (a legal route for sending data abroad).
Limit where the agent can send data. Instructions alone do not stop a send. A sandbox or network limit can.

title: The Locked Cabinet
text:
What stays behind: transcripts
The agent keeps a record of the session so that it can resume. Anything that passes through a tool goes into that record: file contents, command output, pasted text. If a tool reads a .env file or a command prints a credential, the value is written to the session transcript. Transcripts are stored locally in plaintext, for 30 days by default.
In November 2026 a coding-tool vendor reported an incident: an access key issued to one of its vendors was exposed, and a storage bucket held limited coding agent traces. A small number of those traces contained credentials that had not been redacted.
Habits that cost little:

Reference a secret, do not type it. Write psql "$DATABASE_URL", so the command, and any rule saved from it, holds a variable’s name.
Approve patterns, not literal commands (npm run *). When you choose “Yes, and don’t ask again”, Claude Code saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json. On first write in a git repository it adds that file to your global git excludes. If you create the file by hand, add it to .gitignore yourself. Open the file now and then, and delete any saved rule that contains a secret.
Rotate anything that has been in a transcript. Deleting the file does not reach backups, copies or a vendor’s storage.
Keep less. The cleanupPeriodDays setting shortens how long transcripts stay. claude purge deletes a project’s state (try --dry-run first). CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY=1 skips writing transcripts and prompt history.
Make a leak worth little. A token for one repository that expires in an hour is a small loss if it leaks. A GitHub installation access token expires after 1 hour. Where a service only issues long-lived keys, give the agent a separate, narrow key that you can rotate without breaking your own work.

Redaction helps and has limits. A scanner matches formats, and a password after -p has none.

title: The Locked Cabinet
text:
Unpublished ideas and results
A common worry: my unpublished results or ideas will leak and someone will get there first. The habits below lower the chance and the cost of being wrong.
Training use means a provider may learn from your prompts to improve future models. For Claude Code:

For Free, Pro, Max and Ultra accounts, training use depends on a privacy setting that you can change.
For Team, Enterprise and API accounts, code and prompts sent to Claude Code are not used for training under commercial terms, unless the customer opts in.
Retention for consumer accounts is 5 years if you allow model improvement and 30 days if you do not. Commercial accounts have 30 days as standard, and zero data retention for qualified Enterprise accounts.
Read the terms of the exact tool and plan you use, including the privacy page of any chat app. Other providers’ terms differ by product and plan; read the terms for the exact plan you use.

Habits:

Keep unpublished ideas, results and sequences out of consumer chat tools unless the terms say how your text is used and you accept that.
Prefer an agreement your institution has reviewed. Ask your data steward or research office what is approved. They can advise on contracts and ownership.
Consider a local model. Ollama does not see your prompts or data when you run locally. Tools and web calls the model makes may still send data out. A free hosted tier still sends your prompts to a provider.
Date-stamp your work. A preprint, a repository tag or a dated lab notebook entry records when you had it.
Share on a need-to-know basis. Send collaborators what they need for the task.

title: Who Said What
text:
Goal: you will tell the system prompt, the instructions file and your own message apart, and know which you control and which only advise.
Before you start: The Context Window. This is an optional side quest.
Time: about 15 minutes.
When an agent follows a rule, it is fair to ask where that rule came from. The harness is the program around the model that runs tools and sends your text. It works with three common sources of rules, and they differ in who writes them, how long they last and whether anything enforces them.

title: Who Said What
text:
The three voices









Voice
Who writes it
How long it lasts
Can you edit it?




System prompt
The harness
Sent ahead of the conversation on every request
Rarely; you can append or replace it with flags


Instructions file (CLAUDE.md)

In Claude Code, the system prompt is the set of instructions sent ahead of your conversation on every request: how to use tools, behave safely and format answers. Add to it with --append-system-prompt or replace it with --system-prompt.
CLAUDE.md is loaded at the start of every session as a user message after the system prompt (text the model receives in the user’s role). It sits outside the system prompt. Output-style instructions (a setting that changes how the model words its replies) are delivered the same way. Both arrive in the conversation as system reminders (notes the harness slips into the conversation).

title: Who Said What
text:
Rules you did not write
System reminders also carry the skills list, hook additionalContext (text a hook hands back for the harness to add to the conversation), notes about changed files and commit or pull-request attribution lines. A hook is a script the harness runs at set moments, such as just before a tool runs.
If the agent follows a rule you never wrote, for example adding a co-author line to commits, look at what the harness adds on its own first.

title: Who Said What
text:
Advice or enforcement
The instructions file is context that advises. Specific and short instructions are followed more consistently, and longer files use more context and reduce adherence.
To block an action regardless of what the model decides, use enforcement: a PreToolUse hook (a hook that runs at the point just before a tool runs, and is code that enforces the rule) or a deny rule (a settings rule that blocks a named action). Use enforcement for what must never happen.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Reads CLAUDE.md. If a project has only an AGENTS.md (and no CLAUDE.md in or above the working directory), it is read instead, from v2.1.277. To share one file, import it from CLAUDE.md with @AGENTS.md.
