title: When to Start Fresh
text:
Goal: you will name the signals that say “start a new session”, the signals that say “carry on”, and when compacting fits better than either.
Before you start: Memory, Sessions and Usage
Time: about 15 minutes.
You have a conversation open with an agent. It has read files, tried things and been corrected. Do you keep typing into it, or start over? Each answer fits some situations, and a wrong choice costs something either way.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
Words first

Session: one saved conversation with the tool.
Context: the text the model can see right now. It has a fixed size limit.
Compacting: replacing the long history with a short summary and carrying on in the same conversation.
Starting fresh: opening a new, empty conversation. Your files stay as they are.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
Signals to start fresh

A new, unrelated task. Run /clear between unrelated tasks. It costs nothing, and the next task stops paying for the previous one’s history. A session holding three unrelated tasks re-reads all three on every turn of the fourth. A name, as in /clear oauth-migration, labels the conversation you leave so you can find it again.
The agent repeats a wrong claim after two corrections. Clear, and write one better prompt that includes what you learned. A third correction adds to a conversation that already holds two failed attempts.
You notice it forgetting early instructions or contradicting itself. A crowded or degraded context is the usual cause. Start fresh, and move the instruction into the instructions file (CLAUDE.md). Detailed early instructions can also be lost when a conversation is compacted.
You have been away for a while and the next task is new. The tool keeps a cache, a short-term store that makes re-reading the conversation cheaper. It lasts about an hour on a subscription and five minutes with an API key. A very long session (past about 200 thousand tokens) that sits idle may be compacted shortly before the cache expires, so you return to a summary. If you do not need the history, a fresh session costs less.
The context is crowded. Run /context: it shows what fills the window. A crowded window with a task you still need is a reason to compact (below). A crowded window full of dead ends is a reason to clear.
A task is finished and a verified result is committed. The result lives in your files and in git, so the conversation has done its job. The same move works after a spec (a written description of what to build): write it down, then start a fresh session to build from it.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
Signals to carry on

Same task, early decisions still matter: the next step needs the same files, the decisions you made and what was already tried.
The agent is on track: nothing is repeated or contradicted. Clearing a working session throws away good context.
You are returning to a named session: /resume (or claude --resume <name>) reopens a session you chose, and claude --continue reopens the most recent one in this directory. Resume restores the messages, model and permission mode (what the agent may do without asking). Pass startup flags such as --mcp-config again. A compacted session continues from its last summary.
The tool offers to resume after a long break: on some plans a dialog estimates how much of your usage limit the saved conversation would use. Choose by whether your next task still needs it.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
The middle path: compact
/compact replaces the history with a summary and stays in the same conversation. Give it a focus note, as in /compact focus on the auth bug fix, so the summary spends its words on what you still need.

Kept: your requests and key code snippets.
May be lost: detailed instructions from early in the conversation. Restate any that matter.
Re-supplied afterwards: the system prompt, the project-root CLAUDE.md, auto memory and skill descriptions. Up to five recently used files are re-read.
Automatic: the tool also compacts as you approach the limit. A manual /compact lets you choose the moment and the emphasis.
Cost: compacting reads the whole conversation once, so it uses some of your usage.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
The decision ladder








Situation
Action
Why

/clear

/compact with a focus note

Same task, agent on track, plenty of room

Nothing to fix

A third correction sits on two failures

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
Before you clear
Starting fresh drops the conversation. Your files and memory remain, and the instructions file and auto memory load again in the new session. Anything you only said in chat is gone: the decisions, what failed and why, which sample misbehaved. Write that down before you clear, and commit the result so the state is recoverable. If you clear by mistake, /resume can reopen the old conversation.

title: When to Start Fresh
section: The cache and the coffee break
text:
The cache and the coffee break
While the cache is warm, the long history you already sent is re-read cheaply. When it has expired, the next request pays to send the whole history again at full price. A long break in a long session can therefore cost more than you expect.

Run /usage and read what your plan reports about your limits, and about the prompt cache if it reports anything on it.
Before a long break in a long session, run /compact with a focus note, or write a short handoff note (goal, what is done, what is next) and plan to /clear.
After a break, when the next task is new, start fresh.
After a break, when you still need the thread, start a new session from your short note. It lets you drop dead ends too.
Decide your tool set at the start of a task. Changing the built-in tool set in the middle of a task discards the cache.
Trim output before it lands in the conversation. Ask the agent to show only the last lines of a log or a pass/fail summary.

Short pauses are fine. A few minutes away costs little, so there is no need to rush back.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
The cost of both mistakes

Clearing too early loses useful context. The agent must re-read files and rediscover decisions, which costs time and usage, and you may need to repeat yourself.
Clearing too late costs too. The whole conversation is sent again on every request, so usage climbs, and a focused context gives better answers than a crowded one, even with a large window.

Both errors are cheap to recover from if you wrote things down. That is the argument for notes.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Commands for this page: /clear (alias /new), /compact [instructions], /context, /resume [session], claude --continue, claude --resume [name], /rename. Use /context to see how full the window is.


OpenCode has /new (alias /clear), /sessions (aliases /resume, /continue) and /compact (alias /summarize). The same signals apply to any tool, because every model has a finite window. A local model with a smaller window means starting fresh sooner. Run /help in OpenCode to see what else your version offers.

Battle: empty the hopper or not




Next time you notice yourself pasting the same background twice, note it: that was the moment to put it in the instructions file.


At the end of your next working session, write one line saying which signal (new task, repeated error, forgotten instruction, long break, crowded context, finished and committed) would have told you to start fresh, or that none applied.

title: Tokens, Not Letters
text:
Goal: you will explain that a model reads tokens (chunks of text) and decide which sequence jobs belong to a script.
Before you start: Know Your Gear.
Time: about 15 minutes.
You read a read as letters: A, C, G, T. A language model reads tokens. Before your text reaches the model, it is cut into tokens, and the model works with those.

title: Tokens, Not Letters
text:
What a token is
A token is the smallest unit a model works with. It can be a whole word, part of a word, a single character or a byte. Common strings get larger tokens because that is efficient. Rare or unseen words are broken into smaller pieces so the model can still handle them.
Three consequences:

Tokens are not words. A sentence of ten words rarely comes to ten tokens; the count depends on the model and the language.
The count changes between models. Models from Claude 4.7 onward, including Sonnet 5.5, use a newer tokenizer (the part that cuts text into tokens). It produces about 30 percent more tokens for the same text, and the exact increase depends on the content. Count again for each model generation.
Limits and cost are measured in tokens. The context window (all the text a model can look at when it writes its next piece of output) is counted in tokens, and the same prompt can cost different amounts on different models. The API (programmatic access to the model, billed per token, as opposed to a chat plan) has a free token-counting endpoint. Its answer is an estimate that may differ slightly from real use.

title: Tokens, Not Letters
text:
Why this matters for sequences
The model sees chunks of letters, so jobs that depend on every single letter are risky:

Counting letters (“how many Gs in this read”) means counting inside chunks the model cannot see into. Answers are often close and sometimes wrong.
Copying exactly a long string, such as a barcode or an accession, needs a check against the source.
Positions, reverse complements and checksums depend on every single letter.

The exercise below shows how a tokenizer cuts a DNA line.
So the rule: if the answer has to be exact and a rule for it exists, have the agent run a script or a tool and report what it printed. Check any sequence the model retyped against the source file.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Ask it to write and run the counting command and read its output. You can then read the command and the output yourself.


Same advice: ask for the command and read its output. Run the exercise below with your own model and compare.

title: Tokens, Not Letters
text:
Optional exercise (laptop, no real data)
Take this mock line: >read1 ACGTTGCAAGGCTTAGGCCATTAGC. Count the letters yourself with a command you already have, for example echo ACGTTGCAAGGCTTAGGCCATTAGC | grep -o G | wc -l. Then paste the same line and a plain English sentence of similar length into any tokenizer page you trust, or a token counter you have. Compare the token counts. Keep real or sensitive sequences out of web tools.

title: The Context Window
text:
Goal: you will say what fills the context window, what happens when it is full, and three habits that keep it useful.
Before you start: Tokens, Not Letters. A token is a chunk of text the model reads.
Time: about 20 minutes.
The context window is all the text the model can look at when it writes its next piece of output, including its own reply. It works like the model’s working memory and is separate from what the model learned in training. It is measured in tokens.

title: The Context Window
text:
What fills it
In Claude Code (a coding agent that runs in your terminal), the window holds your instructions, the files it reads, its own responses, and content that never appears in your terminal. Before you type anything, it already holds:

the instructions file (CLAUDE.md, a text file the harness loads at session start; the harness is the program around the model that runs tools and sends your text)
auto memory (notes the harness keeps from earlier sessions)
the names of MCP tools (tools added from outside servers) and skill descriptions (short summaries of saved instruction sets)

Every file it reads and every tool output then adds more. At the API level (programmatic access to the model) the same idea holds: the system prompt (the harness’s own instructions, sent with every request), every message, tool results, tool definitions and the output all count.
Sizes depend on the model, up to 1 million tokens for some and 200 thousand for others. A big window gives room for more text, and quality depends on what fills it.

title: The Context Window
text:
Bigger is not better
As the token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade. This is called context rot. Anthropic’s docs give no token count at which it starts, so check the source of any figure you see. What you put in matters as much as how much fits.

title: The Context Window
text:
When it fills up

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


It compacts automatically as the limit nears: the history is replaced by a summary. The summary keeps your requests and key code snippets, but detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost.
Afterwards, Claude Code re-supplies:

the system prompt, the project-root CLAUDE.md, auto memory and skill descriptions
up to five recently read or edited files (a file over 5,000 tokens comes back as a path only)

Nested instruction files are summarised away and reload on demand.
Useful controls:

/context shows what is using space.
/compact with a focus note compacts on purpose.
/clear starts clean between unrelated tasks.

A subagent (a helper agent) has its own window and only a summary comes back. If one file or output is so big that the window refills after every summary, auto-compaction stops with an error.


Check OpenCode’s documentation for how it compacts and how it reports window usage. Expect any tool to drop or summarise something when the window is full. A local model may run with a smaller window, so check your model’s setting.

title: The Context Window
text:
Three habits

Start fresh for a new task. An unrelated earlier thread takes room and can distract.
Keep outputs small. In bioinformatics terms: ask for the head, a count, or a summary script’s output when the file is a big variant table or a whole log.
Put durable facts in the instructions file, such as how to run tests or which folders are off limits. Instructions given only in chat can be lost to compaction. Keep that file short: aim for under 200 lines, because longer files use more context and reduce how well the agent follows them.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
text:
Goal: you will use six terms precisely (token, context window, session context, memory, session usage, context poisoning), and say what to do when a wrong claim has got into a session or into memory.
Before you start: The Context Window. Commands here are Claude Code commands.
Time: about 15 minutes.
People say “it remembers”, “the session got long” and “I hit my usage” as if these were one thing. They are different things, with different places they live and different ways to reset them. Think of a lab glossary: one term, one meaning.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
text:
The glossary

Token: a chunk of text the model reads (a word piece, a character or a byte). Context limits and usage are counted in tokens.
Context window: everything the model can see when it writes its next output. It has a size limit, measured in tokens.
Session and session context: a session is a saved conversation tied to a project directory (stored locally as a transcript file). Its session context is what is in the window right now. Each session begins with a fresh context window, and sessions are independent: a new session has no history from earlier ones.
Memory: text on disk that is read into a new window at the start of every session.
Session usage: how much of your allowance a session consumes.
Context poisoning: a wrong or injected statement enters the context and later answers build on it. The term is community vocabulary. A commonly cited example is a game-playing agent whose recorded goals became corrupted with false state.


Memory in Claude Code
Both kinds are loaded at session start:

CLAUDE.md: instructions you write (the file can be set at project, user or organisation scope: who or where it applies).
Auto memory: notes the harness (the program around the model) writes itself from your corrections and preferences. It is per git repository and machine-local, kept in ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/ as plain markdown with a MEMORY.md index. Only the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md load at start; topic files are read on demand.

Memory is advisory context, and it takes room in the window every session. Run /clear and the conversation goes while memory stays. Compaction (replacing old conversation with a summary) shrinks a session and leaves memory as it was.


Session usage in Claude Code

/usage shows an estimated session cost (worked out locally from token counts at list price, the published per-token price), plan usage limits and activity stats. /cost and /stats are aliases.
The displayed session total resets on /clear. Check your plan’s documentation for when spent allowance resets.
With a subscription, the plan bars are what matter and the dollar figure is an estimate. Plans have usage limit windows; your plan’s documentation gives the exact ones.
With the API, usage is billed per token, and thinking tokens (the tokens the model spends reasoning before it answers) count as output tokens.
For allowance sizes, check the vendor’s pricing page.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
text:
Why usage climbs

Claude Code sends the whole conversation on every request, and each tool-using step is another request.
Caching (a short-term store so repeated text is cheaper to re-read) makes re-reading cheaper, but a short question late in a long session still draws on all of it.
Large tool outputs stay in the conversation. Reading a 10,000-line log is one example.
Subagents (helper agents with their own context window) each have their own context, and their requests still count.
/compact itself reads the whole conversation.
Cached text has a lifetime, and a long break can outlast it, which makes the next message much dearer.

Remedies:

/clear between unrelated tasks.
/compact with a focus note.
/context to see what fills the window.
Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines.

If /usage shows “rate limited until …”, the tool could not fetch your plan limits.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
section: When a wrong claim gets in
text:
When a wrong claim gets in
If you have corrected the same thing twice and it is still wrong, run /clear and write one new prompt that folds in what you learned. A third correction mostly adds to a conversation that already holds two failed attempts for the model to re-read. /rewind can roll back to before the bad turn.
Memory persists, so a wrong line costs the most there. Check a claim against the source, such as the data, the tool’s --help or the paper, before it goes into CLAUDE.md or auto memory. If a bad line is already there, open /memory, read what has been written about your project, and delete it.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Commands:

/memory: lists memory files, toggles auto memory, opens the folder.
/clear: new empty conversation; the old one stays resumable.
/compact: replace the history with a summary.
/resume and claude --resume: pick an earlier session.
claude --continue: the most recent session in this directory.
/usage and /context: usage and window contents.

Resume restores messages, model and permission mode (what the agent may do without asking). Startup flags such as --mcp-config need to be passed again. Transcripts are deleted after 30 days by default.

title: Handoff Notes
text:
Goal: you will list the five things that carry knowledge into a fresh session, and write a short handoff note a fresh session can act on, with what was checked kept apart from what was not.
Before you start: The Stream of Ideas. Commands here are Claude Code commands.
Time: about 15 minutes.
You stop work on Friday with a half-finished refactor. On Monday you open a new session (one conversation with the agent, which has its own context: the text it can see right now). Each session begins with a fresh context window and no memory of what came before, so the new session does not know your goal, what you tried, or what you checked.
Anything it should know has to cross the gap in writing.

title: Handoff Notes
section: Five things that cross the gap
text:
Five things that cross the gap

The instructions file (CLAUDE.md in Claude Code). A file you write that is loaded at the start of every session. Good for stable facts and conventions: how to run the tests, which folders are off limits.
Auto memory. Notes the harness (the program around the model) writes itself, from your corrections and preferences. In Claude Code, /memory lists and opens them.
Files in the repository (the project folder under version control): code, tests, a README, and, if you keep one, a progress or handoff file.
Git history. A commit is a saved snapshot of the project with a message you or the agent write. The list of commits shows what changed and when. It is durable unless rewritten (rebase, amend, force-push), and unpushed commits are local only.
Your handoff note. A short file about the state of one task, written for the next session.











What
Goes where
Lifetime
Who writes it
Trust




Stable rules and conventions
Instructions file
Until you edit it
You
High if short and checked


Preferences the tool picked up
Auto memory
Until deleted
The tool
Medium: it can be wrong


What the files say now
Files in the repository
Until edited or deleted
You or the agent
Medium: files can be stale


State of one task
Handoff note
Until the task is done
You, or the agent drafts and you review
Only as good as your review


What changed, and why
Commit messages in git history
Durable unless rewritten; local until pushed
You or the agent
Reliable for what changed; the why is only as good as the message



Memory the tool wrote can be wrong, and a wrong line is loaded again every session. This is context poisoning: a wrong statement enters the context and later answers build on it. Read /memory and check any claim against the source before you rely on it.
Three habits help a long task: keep a progress notes file, make git commits with descriptive messages so bad changes can be reverted, and begin each session by reading the progress file and the recent git log, then run a basic check before new work.

title: Handoff Notes
section: What a good handoff note contains
text:
What a good handoff note contains
Keep it short, so reading it costs less than rediscovering the state. Point to files and commands, and let the next session run them for fresh output.

Goal in one line.
Current state: branch, last commit, what runs and what does not.
Decisions and the reasons, including options you rejected.
Verified, and how; not verified. Two separate lists. For each verified item, the command and what it showed.
What failed and should not be retried.
Next steps, in order.
Pointers: file paths, commands, job IDs, work directories.
Open questions and parked ideas (ideas you decided to leave for later).

title: Handoff Notes
text:
Mock example
This is a mock handoff note for a mock task. The file names and numbers are invented.
# HANDOFF: qc_filter.py refactor (mock example)

## Goal
Replace the per-read loop in qc_filter.py with a vectorised version, same output.

## State (git branch refactor-qc, last commit a1b2c3d "qc: add vectorised mean quality")
- New function mean_qual_fast() is written and called from main().
- Old function mean_qual() is kept for comparison. Do not delete yet.

## Decisions
- Keep both functions until all samples are compared (a bug here would silently change which reads pass).
- Threshold stays at mean Q20, as in the lab protocol.

## Verified
- tests/test_filter.py: ran `pytest -q`, 6 passed.
- sample_A: `diff <(python qc_filter.py A.fq) old_out/A.txt` gave no output.

## Not verified
- Samples B and C have not been compared with the old output.
- Reads shorter than 30 bases: no test covers them.
- Speed gain: not measured.

## Failed, do not retry
- Using numpy on the raw quality string: wrong values for the Phred offset. Convert to integers first.

## Next steps
1. Compare B and C against old_out/ with the same diff command.
2. Add a test for a 10-base read.
3. Only then delete mean_qual().

## Open questions / parked
- Should the threshold be a command-line option? Parked for a later task.

title: Handoff Notes
section: Where to put it, and how to start the next session
text:
Where to put it, and how to start the next session
Put the note in a file the next session can find. Two options:

A file in the repo, such as HANDOFF.md, if the team should see it.
A gitignored ordinary file you point to, if it is personal. This is the simpler choice.

CLAUDE.local.md at the project root (add it to .gitignore) holds private per-project preferences and loads after CLAUDE.md. It exists only in the worktree where you created it.
Anything loaded every session takes room in the window, so keep a handoff note out of CLAUDE.md and remove it once its task is done.
Write the note before you run /clear (which starts a new empty conversation), because /clear drops the conversation. Pairing the note with a commit leaves a matching record in git.
Then start the new session with a prompt like this:

Read HANDOFF.md, then tell me your understanding before changing anything.

The agent restates the goal and state in its own words, and you compare that with what you know. This is a cheap comprehension check: it can catch a misreading of the note. The restatement comes from the same model that read it, so the note’s claims still need checking against the source.
You can ask the agent to draft the note at the end of a session. Review it yourself, since a draft can overstate what was verified (“all tests pass” when none were run in that session).

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Commands:

/memory: see memory files.
/clear: new empty conversation.
/resume and claude --resume: reopen an earlier session.
claude --continue: the most recent session in this directory.
/export: writes the conversation as plain text for a person to read. Transcripts are long, so write a short curated note yourself.



Commands: /new (alias /clear), /sessions (aliases /resume and /continue), /compact and /export. The handoff note itself is just a file, so the practice carries over. Check OpenCode’s documentation for how it loads project instructions, and keep the note short if your local model has a small window.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
Goal: you will keep heavy work and sprawling searches off the shared login node and shared storage, and hand heavy work to the scheduler.
Before you start: Grow the Carapace. A login node is the shared machine you log in to. Compute nodes run your jobs. The scheduler (here Slurm) decides which job runs where.
Time: about 15 minutes.
Ask your cluster staff before running an agent on the login node. Some sites forbid agents on login nodes altogether, so follow your cluster’s user guide where it differs from this page. This quest is read-only, so read it on your laptop.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
Login node versus compute node
Everyone who logs in shares the login node. The scheduler places your jobs on compute nodes. Light work (editing text, git, listing one directory, checking a log with head or tail) is normally fine on the login node. Heavy work belongs on compute nodes: aligners, long foreground pipelines, compressing or indexing big files, building large environments, or running a test suite at scale.
An agent does not know which node it is on or what your site tolerates. It will run a long command if you let it, so you set the rule. It also misjudges “this will only take a few seconds”, so tell it to ask when a command’s cost is unclear.
Some sites allow agents only inside an interactive compute allocation, and some run a different scheduler with its own commands. If a scheduler command is missing, ask staff and skip near-matches.
A long-running helper process left on the login node, even one that only hands tasks to the scheduler, is not always allowed. Check your site’s policy first.
If the agent has a question for you and you are away, a good agent stops and lists its open questions. Ask for that in your instructions: do the steps that need no answer, stop, and list the questions.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
Shared storage prefers scoped searches
Network filesystems can slow down for everyone when something touches huge numbers of files. Agents explore by searching, so a careless find / or a recursive grep -r from your home or project root is the classic mistake. Ask for searches scoped to one known directory, and keep them away from /. The same goes for du, ls --recursive, ls --format=long (it stats every file) and wide globs on big directories, and avoid making many small files in one directory. Keep the agent to your own project paths: other users’ or other projects’ paths are off limits unless you named them or the site documents them as shared (reference data).
Claude Code’s search tools (Glob, Grep) are not a filesystem-load control; scope the search yourself.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
The scheduler’s four commands
Four commands cover most of it:



Command
What it does




sbatch
submit a job script; returns a job ID


srun
run a job or job step in real time


squeue
report the state of jobs


scancel
cancel a pending or running job



sbatch --test-only validates a script and estimates a start time. No job is submitted, so it works as a dry run. Slurm’s default time limit is the partition’s default, so set limits in the script.
Set --time, --mem and --cpus-per-task, and use a job array for many similar tasks. Write options in their long form (--dry-run for -n) so you can read what the agent proposes.
Slurm bills by what you allocate, whatever you use. A memory request can change how many CPUs Slurm allocates, because partitions limit memory per CPU (MaxMemPerCPU). Above that limit Slurm may raise the CPU count to fit, or reject the job. Read the partition’s limits, and afterwards compare request, allocation and use with sacct.
Scratch space holds throwaway files. Ask your staff where the project’s scratch is, tell the agent, and use it instead of /tmp, which is shared on a login node and often small. Inside a job, use a temporary directory only if your site documents one, and copy results to the project directory before the job ends. A set $TMPDIR does not prove you are on scratch, because Slurm can set it to /tmp. Scripts, logs and final outputs stay in the project directory.

title: Login Node Manners
section: Look before you copy or delete
text:
Look before you copy or delete
Find out what a copy or a delete will touch before it touches anything. Run rsync --dry-run --itemize-changes first, with the same arguments, and read the list. Does it match your request? Does it hold keys, .env files or personal data? Does a *deleting line remove something you wanted to keep? cp, scp and rm have no dry run, so list the exact path or glob and delete only those names. Any change to the options needs a new dry run. Do not copy from or delete a directory that a running job writes to. Before you delete a source you copied, repeat the copy as a dry run with --checksum and delete only if the list is empty. Options such as --exclude skip files without a word. rsync --delete and rm --recursive also remove what is inside a directory, so list and dry-run those too. The dry run reads the whole tree like the real run, so run it where the real run will run. Send large transfers through the scheduler or the site’s data-transfer node.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
What the agent’s sandbox covers

Claude Code’s sandbox covers shell commands only. File tools, MCP servers and hooks run outside it.
It fails open by default: if it cannot start, commands run without sandboxing, unless sandbox.failIfUnavailable is true.
On Linux it needs bubblewrap and socat. You usually cannot install packages system-wide on a cluster, so ask staff whether they are installed.
Check that the sandbox is on before you rely on it.


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Tell the agent where it may run what, in your project instructions or the prompt, and back it with a permission rule where you can. Useful instructions:

“Search only inside ./workflow/. Never run find or grep -r from / or $HOME.”
“Run nothing in the foreground on the login node. Draft an sbatch script and show it to me.”

Instructions are guidance, and the agent can still slip. If a project instruction file (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md) is stricter than these lines, the stricter one wins.
Foreground commands time out (default 2 minutes, maximum 10 by default), so a long-running foreground command in the agent’s shell is cut off anyway.


The same habits apply. OpenCode’s permission model uses allow, ask and deny rules, and an unmatched action asks. Its base policy begins with an allow-all rule, so sbatch runs without a prompt until you add a rule. Add explicit rules for the cluster commands, and check your installed version’s permission docs. A local model through Ollama runs on the node you are on and touches the filesystem the same way.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
text:
Goal: you will let the agent draft job scripts while you keep submitting and cancelling under your own approval, you will know what polling costs, and you will size resource requests against the partition’s limits.
Before you start: Login Node Manners. A job script is a text file of scheduler options and commands. Polling means asking the scheduler for status again and again.
Time: about 20 minutes.
Ask your cluster staff before letting an agent near your cluster account, and follow your cluster’s policy and data agreement over this page. This quest is read-only, so read it on your laptop.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
text:
Draft versus submit
A job script is text. Letting an agent draft one is low risk, because you read it before anything runs. Submitting spends shared resources, and cancelling can destroy work. A sensible split:

The agent drafts scripts and may check state (squeue, sinfo, sacct). Limit sacct with --jobs=<jobid> or --starttime=<date> so it does not dump the whole accounting history.
You approve sbatch, srun, salloc and scancel.

Before approving an sbatch, read the script and the resource request: --time, --mem, and the array size if it is an array.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
Jobs, Not Jam
section: Why scancel -u is the dangerous one
text:
Why scancel -u is the dangerous one
scancel -u <you> signals all your jobs, including ones the agent did not submit. Whole jobs are terminated, and other work of yours dies with them. scancel --me does the same. The man page lists more bulk selectors: --name, --state, --partition, plus account, QOS, reservation and node list. Each acts on every job it matches, and combined filters must all match. Deny rules cannot cover every spelling, so the single ask rule on scancel * is the net and the deny rules catch the worst two. Use scancel <jobid> for an ID the agent itself submitted. Slurm can rate-limit a user whose requests arrive at a sustained high rate, so a runaway loop of commands is a problem for the scheduler as well as for you.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
text:
Polling costs money and attention
Claude Code charges by token use. The whole conversation is sent with every request, and each tool use sends another request. A /loop (a command that re-runs a prompt on a timer) that polls squeue keeps firing on its interval, even while the session is idle, and sends your full context each time. Verbose output such as long logs also inflates the context.
The scheduler pays too. The squeue and sacct manual pages warn against running them from loops, because it can slow slurmctld (the scheduler daemon) or slurmdbd (the accounting database) for everyone.
Habits that keep polling cheap:

Poll no more than about once a minute, less often for long jobs. Run one loop at a time and scope it: squeue --user=$USER or --jobs=<id>.
Use sbatch --parsable --wait, or the pipeline’s own poller, instead of a sleep loop. It replaces a /loop of squeue, so skip the loop.
A wait can outlast the tool’s timeout. Run it in the background. Never resubmit because the wait timed out. Check State with sacct first: --wait passes the job’s exit code through, but a signal-killed job gives 1, so the code alone does not prove success.
--mail-type sends you an email and does not make the agent wait. If you use watch, keep it at --interval=60 or slower and stop it when done.
Submit many similar tasks as one array with a concurrency cap (--array=1-100%10) instead of a loop of sbatch calls.

Foreground commands in Claude Code time out (default 2 minutes, maximum 10 by default), so an agent waiting on a long foreground command, such as an srun that blocks until it finishes, gets cut off.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
text:
Size the request
A job can use more of the cluster than you meant to ask for, and no error tells you. Slurm counts what you allocate, whatever you use, and that count feeds your fair-share priority (how soon your later jobs start). A partition is a group of nodes with its own limits. Many partitions limit memory per CPU (MaxMemPerCPU), so a large memory request on one CPU can make Slurm add CPUs to fit it, or reject the job. A request like --mem=120G with MaxMemPerCPU=4000 (MB) can become about 31 CPUs. Other limit settings can leave an over-limit job pending instead, so read what your site does.
Habits that keep requests honest:

Before a large or repeated job, read the partition’s limits (scontrol show partition <name>) and size the request against them. Pick a number from the limits and from earlier runs.
Afterwards compare what you asked for, what was allocated and what was used: sacct --jobs=<id> --format=JobID,State,ReqMem,AllocCPUS,MaxRSS. MaxRSS (the most memory one task used) is filled on the step rows such as .batch. Keep headroom above it. If sacct prints nothing, accounting may be off, so say so and ask your staff.
A job killed for memory can show OUT_OF_MEMORY in State. MaxRSS then understates the need, so raise the request above the failed one.
If the memory need and the CPU count conflict, ask staff for a partition with a better memory-to-CPU ratio and check with them before using it.

title: Three Kinds of Machine
text:
Goal: you will tell apart a deterministic program, a trained model and an LLM, and pick the right one for a job.
Before you start: Name the Fears.
Time: about 10 minutes.

title: Three Kinds of Machine
text:
Three kinds

A deterministic program (a script, awk, samtools): the same input always gives the same output, and you can read why. Use it whenever the rule is known.
A trained model (a classifier, a gene-finder, a structure predictor): learned from data to do one task, with measured accuracy on that task. It is the predictive side of AI: it forecasts from past data and gives you an estimate to act on. Use it when the rule is unknown but the task is narrow and validated.
A large language model (LLM): trained on large amounts of text, then tuned to follow instructions. It is the generative side of AI: it produces new content (text, code, images) that you review, flexible and fluent, with no built-in guarantee of correctness. Use it where the task is open-ended and you can check the result, such as drafting, explaining, or writing a first version of code that you then test.

The line between the last two is not clean. An LLM can be asked to classify, and some generative models predict structure or sequences. Judge a tool by the task you give it and how you will check the result. For a forecast, a simpler predictive model usually does the job more cheaply than a generative one.
Two common mistakes: using an LLM to do something a one-line script does exactly (slow, costly, and sometimes wrong), and trusting a model outside the task it was validated for.
An LLM can also be called inside a script (for example to tidy free-text labels). That makes your pipeline non-deterministic, so the result needs its own checks and the exact model and version recorded.
Before you reach for an agent or a large model, ask whether a script, a fixed workflow or a smaller specialised model does the job. A method that fits the task is often cheaper to run and easier to reproduce, and it does not change when a provider updates a hosted model. Keep the large model for the open-ended steps.
Fine-tuning a model on your own examples suits only some tasks.

title: Three Kinds of Machine
section: What a model can do on its own
text:
What a model can do on its own
A language model with no tools suits some jobs and struggles with others. A large hosted model will do better than a small one on some rows.







Suits
Struggles with




Summarising and editing text
Counting letters or basic arithmetic


Pulling out names and places
Multi-step logical reasoning


Classifying a piece of text
Facts it was never given


Generating tags, short creative writing
Writing code (a small on-device model)



Harder tasks become possible once the model can call tools or produce structured output. That is the idea behind an agent: the model reads and writes, and a harness gives it tools (a shell, a file editor, a script runner) for the parts it finds hard. Counting and arithmetic are good work to hand to a script.

title: Know Your Gear
text:
Goal: you will use the words this site relies on (model, harness, skill, MCP, hook, plugin, effort, eval and the context terms below) and say how they fit together.
Before you start: Three Kinds of Machine.
Time: about 15 minutes.
People mix these words up, and the mix-ups cause real mistakes, such as blaming “the model” for something a setting did. Other tools name things differently; the ideas carry over. In this world the companions are models, and the harness is their armour.

title: Know Your Gear
text:
The picture



How model, harness and extensions relate

A large box named harness contains a smaller box named model, with an effort dial on the model. Inside the harness are tools, permissions, and the loop with context. A row of extensions sits in the harness: skill, MCP, hook, and plugin which bundles them. Outside the harness an eval measures results by running with and without an extension. To the right, the same model is shown inside two different harnesses.   HARNESS (the armour)  MODEL (companion) reads text, writes text  EFFORT: how much it thinks per step Tools: read, edit Permissions Loop, context EXTENSIONS you plug in SKILL MCP HOOK  PLUGIN: a bundle of the above INSTRUCTIONS  EVAL: run with and without, compare  TWO HARNESSES  Model Xinside harness A  Model Xinside harness B Different tools, permission rules and loop, so the same model can behave differently. Claude Code and OpenCode are two harnesses. 


Models think. The harness decides what they can touch and runs the loop. Extensions change what the harness offers. Evals measure from outside. Text version below.

title: Know Your Gear
text:
The words

Model. The large language model (LLM) that reads and writes text (for example Claude Sonnet 5.5, a Mistral model, or a local model through Ollama, a program that runs models on your own computer). The product you type into is the harness. Aliases such as sonnet move to newer versions over time, so pin the full name when a result must be reproducible.
Harness. The program around the model. It provides the tools, manages the context the model sees, runs the loop (gather context, act, check, repeat) and enforces permissions. Claude Code, OpenCode (an open-source harness) and Mistral Vibe (Mistral’s open-source terminal coding agent) are harnesses. Many questions are really about the harness: what may it touch, what does it remember, what does it ask first?
Prompt. The text you send to the model.
Turn. One prompt from you plus the model’s reply.
Agent. A model inside a harness that picks and runs tools in a loop toward a goal.
Tool. An action the model can request and the harness runs, such as reading a file or running a shell command. A tool call is one such request; tool output is what comes back. The program you run is also called “the tool”; that is the harness.
Subagent. A helper agent with its own context window; only its summary comes back.
Instructions file. A text file (CLAUDE.md in Claude Code, AGENTS.md in OpenCode where read) that the harness loads at session start. It advises and does not enforce.
Sandbox. An operating-system layer that limits what commands can touch. A scratch folder is a throwaway directory.
Hallucination (also called a Mirage). A plausible-looking statement that is false, such as an invented DOI (a paper’s permanent identifier).
Prompt injection. Text from a file, web page or tool that the model treats as an instruction.
Skill. A folder with a SKILL.md. Only its short description is preloaded; the body loads when it is used. It advises.
MCP (Model Context Protocol). An open standard for connecting the harness to outside tools and data, such as a database or a literature search. A server you connect can act on your behalf, so treat it like software you install.
Hook. Your own command, request or prompt that the harness runs automatically at a set point, such as before a tool call. A command hook that exits with code 2 before a tool runs stops that action whatever the model wants (a nonzero exit code is how a script signals failure; a hook uses 2 to mean block). A rule in an instructions file can only ask, so hooks are the stronger guard.
Plugin. A folder that bundles skills, hooks, MCP servers and more, installed as one unit. It can run code, so it is a trust decision.
Effort. A setting for how much the model reasons per step, from low to max in Claude Code (/effort, --effort; a /command is typed inside the running tool, a --flag when you start it). Low is faster and cheaper; high thinks longer and checks more. It guides behaviour and sets no exact budget. max can show diminishing returns and overthink, so raise it only where you measure a gain. Higher effort makes answers more careful, and correctness is still yours to check.
Eval. A repeatable test of agent behaviour: a prompt plus checks on the result. Comparing runs with and without something (a skill, a rule) shows what it contributed. A score of 100% both ways means it contributed nothing.

title: Know Your Gear
section: Words about what the model can see
text:
Words about what the model can see
These get mixed up more than any others.

Token. The chunk of text a model actually reads and writes. Somewhere between a letter and a word. Limits and costs are counted in tokens.
Context window. Everything the model can see at once right now: instructions, files it has read, tool output and the conversation so far. It has a size limit, and a fuller window is not automatically a better one.
Session (session context). One running conversation, and the context window it has built up. A new session starts with an empty conversation. Two sessions do not share their context.
Memory. Notes that the harness loads at the start of every session, such as your instructions file and, in Claude Code, notes the tool writes itself. Memory outlives a session; session context does not.
Compaction. The harness replaces old conversation with a summary to free room.
Session usage. How much of your allowance or bill a session spends. It climbs with the size of the context, because the whole conversation is sent again with each request.
Context poisoning. A community term: a wrong statement gets into the context, and later answers build on it. Start a fresh session and keep unverified claims out of memory files.

Naming differs between tools. Check another tool’s docs for how its hooks, plugins and effort settings work.

Redraw the picture from memory for the tool you actually use: which model, which harness, which extensions are loaded right now?

title: Name the Fears
text:
Goal: you will name what worries you about large language model (LLM) agents and pick the habit that answers each worry, whether you plan to use them or not.
Before you start: nothing.
Time: about 10 minutes.

title: Name the Fears
text:
Where people start
People come to these tools from different places:

Some are keen and want to know how to begin well.
Some are curious and want to see what is involved before deciding.
Some hold back, often for good reasons: the environmental cost of AI, harm to people and their work, or the quality of what comes out.

Every one of these starting points is reasonable, and nothing here asks you to use these tools. This odyssey leaves the larger questions to you. It covers the practical worries that come with using an agent and gives each one a habit that makes the risk smaller. Whether you go on to use agents or decide to leave them alone, you will have a clear picture of what they ask of you.
An agent is a model running inside a program that picks and runs tools in a loop toward a goal. A prompt is the text you send to the model. The rest of the odyssey trains the habits below, and each row links to the zone that teaches it.

About the output



The worry
The habit
Where you learn it




“It makes things up.”
Check against something the agent did not write.
Sequence Maze


“It produces slop in bulk.”
Take small steps, test before code, keep a review budget.
Sequence Maze: Wall of Output


“I do not understand what it did.”
Ask for a changelog and explain it back.
Sequence Maze: Keep a Paper Trail



Slop is low-quality bulk output. A review budget means you only produce as much as you can honestly review today.


About the work and your data



The worry
The habit
Where you learn it




“It could delete or overwrite my work.”
Undo with git, set permission rules, work on a scratch copy.
Ancient DNA Crypt


“It could leak my data or my secrets.”
Keep secrets and private data out of prompts; use an approved account or a local model.
Ancient DNA Crypt


“Someone could see my unpublished results and publish first.”
Read your tool’s data terms; keep unpublished work out of consumer chat tools.
Ancient DNA Crypt



A sandbox is an operating-system layer that limits what commands can touch; it is one way to protect your files. For unpublished work, prefer an agreement your institution has reviewed or a local model, and date-stamp your work.


About you and the people around you



The worry
The habit
Where you learn it




“It will stop me learning.”
Write it first, predict before you look, ask it to explain.
Biodiversity Reef


“Someone else has to review all this.”
Review it yourself first, say you used an LLM, send small changes.
Biodiversity Reef


“It will feel hollow, as if it was not my work.”
Make the decisions, explain each step, keep a decision log.
Biodiversity Reef


“Everyone will expect work faster now.”
Say where the time goes; agree timelines that include review.
Biodiversity Reef


“Everything I write will sound the same.”
Draft in your own words first, then edit.
Biodiversity Reef


“I will spend my days checking drafts.”
Keep the question and interpretation; count checking as work.
Biodiversity Reef


“People will think I am lazy or unoriginal.”
Say what the agent did and what you checked.
Biodiversity Reef


“I will stop trusting my own judgement.”
Decide first, then ask for a second opinion.
Biodiversity Reef



For voice and judgement, use the agent for structure and checks, and keep a few decisions agent-free. For credit and workload, follow your team’s norm, credit the agent’s part openly and share how long checking took.
Sometimes the right answer is to skip the LLM. Part of the skill is knowing when.

title: Wade In
text:
Goal: you will choose how much of your data and your machine to hand over for one task, and start at the lowest step that gets the job done.
Before you start: Know Your Gear, and Python 3 for the exercise. Your own data agreement overrides anything here.
Time: about 20 minutes.

title: Wade In
text:
The scene
A manager needs a status report across projects, kept in a spreadsheet. A data analyst needs a count of samples received per project from the project database, using SQL (the language for querying a database). Both have two worries: where the data goes, and the belief that using an LLM means letting an agent loose on their computer.
Between “never” and “the agent runs my machine” there are several steps, and many useful tasks sit on the lower ones. You may stop at any step.

title: Wade In
text:
Two dials

What leaves your machine? With a hosted model, anything you type, paste or upload is sent to the provider, and so is anything an agent reads. A local model keeps prompts on your machine, though web or tool calls it makes may still reach out.
What may the tool do? Produce text, read files, edit files, or run commands.

Each dial needs its own decision. A chat window has a low second dial and can still send a whole pasted table. A read-only agent (it can read files but not change them) sends whatever it reads.

text:
Three questions before any step

What kind of data is it? The table gives a typical starting point. Your agreement and your data steward decide, and they can be stricter. A data steward is the person at your organisation who looks after data rules.
Which account will you use? Consumer and organisation accounts have different terms (next section).
What leaves at this step? Say it in one sentence before you press enter.

Pseudonymised codes still count as personal data. Small counts can single people out, so check your policy before pasting results for rare groups. Real or personal data is not pasted into consumer chat.

title: Wade In
text:
What a chat window keeps

Training: consumer accounts (Free, Pro, Max) have a setting that lets chats improve the models; with it on, data may be kept for up to 5 years. The setting is in your privacy settings.
Account type: commercial accounts (such as Claude for Work and the API) are not used for training and delete inputs and outputs within 30 days by default. Check the plan in your account settings, or ask your administrator.
Deleted chats: they leave the provider’s storage within 30 days.
Incognito chats: not used for training, and still kept for 30 days by default.
Screenshots, images and uploads: treat them as data you share, like pasted text.
Other providers: their chat tools have their own terms. Read them.

Hands-on (data analyst): count samples without handing over the data
Save make_db.py, run_query.py, report-query.sql and check-samples.sql into an empty folder. Every row is invented, and no LLM is called.

Run python3 make_db.py (or python). It writes mock.db and schema-only.txt. The text file holds table and column names and no rows, which is all that goes into a chat at step 2. This table-and-column outline is the schema. Names such as participant_code and notes hint at the real data, so decide whether even the names are fine to send.
Write the prompt you would send: paste the schema and ask for one read-only query giving, per project, the samples received and the open milestones (done = 0). Say you will run it yourself and do not want to paste rows.
report-query.sql stands in for the reply. Check it is a single SELECT (a query that only reads) on the tables you expect, then run python3 run_query.py report-query.sql. The script opens the database read-only, so a DELETE fails.
Run python3 run_query.py check-samples.sql, a count the model did not write, and compare:

The query ran without an error and its numbers are wrong. Each project has two open milestones, and the join (how two tables are matched row by row) pairs every sample with every open milestone, so each sample is counted twice. Fix the query, then run both again until Heron shows 11 and 2.

Only the schema and the query text left your machine. Running without an error and being right are separate questions, so check against a second query.

section: Hands-on (manager): the same check in a spreadsheet
text:
Hands-on (manager): the same check in a spreadsheet
At step 2, paste only the column headings (Project, Milestone, Owner, Status) and two or three invented rows, and ask for a formula that counts open milestones per project. Apply it to your real sheet yourself. Check it with COUNTIF on one project’s rows. If each of three projects has 6 rows and the formula shows 18 for every project, it counted the whole column. Find out why before the number goes in the report.

section: Climbing, if and when you want to
text:
Climbing, if and when you want to

Move up a step when the lower step cannot do the task and you can say what leaves.
Before steps 4 and 5, work on a copy, keep a way to undo, and limit what the agent may do.
For sensitive data, stay on a local model when your agreement allows that copy.

title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
Goal: you will keep keys and agent settings private on shared storage, keep data within its agreement, and know what to ask your cluster staff.
Before you start: Login Node Manners and The Locked Cabinet. Egress means data leaving the machine.
Time: about 15 minutes.
Ask your cluster staff before sending any cluster data to an external model API, and follow your institution’s data agreement. This quest is read-only, so read it on your laptop.

title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
What lives where
Claude Code keeps sessions, settings and plugins in ~/.claude, and writes ~/.claude.json (account details, MCP configuration, trust decisions). CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR relocates the first of these.
If your home directory is shared across nodes, session history sits on shared storage and can contain pasted data or paths. Check who can read it (for example chmod 700 ~/.claude) and whether home is backed up or group-readable.
Settings files: user ~/.claude/settings.json, project .claude/settings.json (commit it), local .claude/settings.local.json, and managed settings. Precedence is managed, then command line, then local, then shared project, then user. Permission lists merge across files. An organisation can enforce managed settings that your own files cannot override, so your site may already have decided some of this.

title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
Keys

ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, when set, overrides a subscription login. In -p (non-interactive) mode it is always used, and interactive mode asks you once to approve it. If a key is exported in a shared profile, the key in use may not be the one you expect.
Never put a key in a script or in a committed .claude/settings.json. On a shared account, use a per-user key kept in a file readable only by you (mode 600), and keep a lab-wide key out of shared directories.
The sandbox’s default reads cover most of the machine, including credential files such as ~/.ssh and ~/.aws/credentials. Use Read(...) deny rules or sandbox.filesystem.denyRead for key files. Remember that the sandbox covers shell commands only.

Look up where OpenCode stores keys, and what the apiKeyHelper setting does, in the docs for your version before you rely on either.

title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
Data and egress

Before any cluster data, paths, logs or code go to an external model API, check your institution’s policy. Human genomic, clinical or controlled-access data often has agreements that forbid third-party processing.
Read is auto-approved inside the working directory, so the agent can read a project folder that holds controlled data unless a Read(...) deny rule or sandbox.filesystem.denyRead covers it. Keep controlled data outside the agent’s working directory and give the agent synthetic or de-identified test data.
Some sites restrict internet access from compute nodes, so an agent there may not reach a model API. Ask staff what outbound access your jobs have. A common pattern is the agent on your laptop writing scripts, with jobs running offline.
A plain ssh from inside the Claude Code sandbox does not work as a hop.
The sandbox’s network.allowedDomains starts empty, so unlisted hosts prompt (in the default modes).


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


If your project has an instruction file (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md) stricter than these notes, the stricter one wins, and your cluster’s policy outranks both. Ask staff these before use: is an external model API allowed for my data, which tools are allowed on login nodes, what outbound access exists, and where are my home and scratch backed up and who can read them? For restricted networks, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 turns off auto-updates, telemetry, error reporting and feedback traffic.


The same questions apply. Ask staff whether a local model through Ollama changes what your data agreement requires, and whether running one on a login node is allowed, since models are heavy. Find where OpenCode keeps its keys in your version’s docs.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
Goal: you will build a small knowledge graph from twelve mock lab notes with a local model, query it, compare it with simple RAG, and learn what LightRAG and Microsoft GraphRAG ask of an Ollama setup.
Before you start: RAG and Its Cousins, and Adopt the Pet (Ollama installed and running). Python 3 on your path; the scripts use only its standard library. This is an optional side quest.
Time: about 30 minutes, most of it waiting for the model. Everything stays on your machine, and the notes are mock data.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
Words first

Simple RAG: embed every note, embed the question, keep the k closest notes, and ask the model to answer from them.
Knowledge graph: facts stored as (subject, relation, object) triples. Things are nodes and the links between them are edges.
Hop: one step along an edge from one entity to a linked one.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
Set up
mini-rag holds ollama_min.py (two helpers), rag.py (simple RAG), graph.py (a hand-made graph RAG) and notes/ (twelve short mock notes, 233 words in all). Save the folder anywhere. If the link is not available, ask your agent to recreate it from the descriptions below.
Pull an embedding model and pick a chat model you already have.
ollama pull nomic-embed-text
export CHAT_MODEL=gemma4:12b-mlx      # or any chat model you have pulled
cd mini-rag
The scripts read three environment variables: CHAT_MODEL, EMBED_MODEL (default nomic-embed-text) and OLLAMA_URL (default http://127.0.0.1:11434). Ollama’s default context is small, so the scripts send each request with num_ctx set to 8192 and you do not have to restart the server.
Open notes/ and read a few. They are fictional: two sequencers (Orion and Vega), two projects (Heron and Kelp), two pipeline releases, and some distractors such as the lunch rota. One question needs a chain of four hops: Project Heron studies samples S31 to S36, run R7 loaded those samples, run R7 used pipeline release 2.3, and release 2.3 has a known bug.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
Step 1: simple RAG
rag.py is simple RAG in about thirty lines.
python3 rag.py "Does project Heron need to re-analyse its data because of a known pipeline bug?"
With the default -k 3 the run printed:
Retrieved:
  0.668  pipeline-2-4.txt
  0.653  pipeline-2-3.txt
  0.644  project-heron.txt

Answer:
The notes do not contain the answer.
The notes that hold the answer were in the folder, but the run log that connects Heron’s samples to pipeline 2.3 ranked fourth. Try -k 5:
  0.668  pipeline-2-4.txt
  0.653  pipeline-2-3.txt
  0.644  project-heron.txt
  0.549  run-r7.txt
  0.528  run-r8.txt

Answer:
Yes, project Heron needs to re-analyse its data because the primary analysis of run R7 used pipeline release 2.3, which has a known bug that double-counts duplicate reads.
Then try --all, which skips retrieval and pastes every note into the prompt. It also gave a correct answer. With twelve short notes, the window holds everything.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
Step 2: build the graph
graph.py build sends each note to the chat model and asks for (subject, relation, object) facts. It uses Ollama’s structured outputs: the request carries a JSON schema in the format field, so the reply is JSON in the shape the script expects. Temperature 0 gives more deterministic output, and the helper sets it.
python3 graph.py build
python3 graph.py show
The run printed saved 67 facts, and the build took 1 minute 20 seconds for twelve notes. A sample of what show printed:
Run R7 --loaded onto--> Orion    [run-r7.txt]
Run R7 --used--> Pipeline 2.3    [run-r7.txt]
Pipeline 2.3 --has bug--> double-counts duplicate reads    [pipeline-2-3.txt]
Project Heron --studies--> S31    [project-heron.txt]
Orion --looked after by--> Dana Okafor    [orion.txt]
You --bring--> own cup    [lunch.txt]
Read the whole list. Most facts match their notes. Two did not: the lunch note produced You --bring--> own cup, which is not a fact about anything in the lab, and one name came back with a stray leading space, which would split a single entity into two nodes (the script now strips names when it loads them). Extraction is a model’s reading of your text, so a graph is a second thing to check. Every fact carries the note it came from, so you can.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
Step 3: ask the graph
graph.py ask does three things. It finds starting entities (names that appear in the question, plus the three closest by embedding). It walks outward two hops along the links. Then it hands the collected facts and their source notes to the model.
python3 graph.py ask "Does project Heron need to re-analyse its data because of a known pipeline bug?"
Starting entities: ['pipeline 2.3', 'pipeline 2.4', 'project heron']
Collected 40 facts from 8 notes: freezers.txt, meeting-march.txt, pipeline-2-3.txt, pipeline-2-4.txt, project-heron.txt, project-kelp.txt, run-r7.txt, run-r8.txt

Answer:
Yes, Project Heron needs to re-analyse its data because Run R7, which loaded the samples for Project Heron (S31 to S36), used Pipeline 2.3, which has a known bug that double-counts duplicate reads.

Notes used:
- [pipeline-2-3.txt]
- [project-heron.txt]
- [run-r7.txt]
The wording of the answer differs a little from run to run even at temperature 0, so yours will not match word for word.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
What we saw
With gemma4:12b-mlx for chat and nomic-embed-text for embeddings:

Simple RAG missed at k=3 and succeeded at k=5. The run log was not among the top three notes. Raising k fixed it, at the price of more text in the prompt.
Putting everything in the prompt also worked, because the collection is tiny.
The graph walk reached the run log without a bigger k, because the link from Heron’s samples to run R7 is an edge. It also pulled in 40 of the 67 facts and 8 of the 12 notes. A bigger collection needs a smaller hop count or a ranking step.
The graph took a minute and twenty seconds to build for 233 words and needs a model good enough to extract facts. Embedding twelve notes for simple RAG takes seconds. Build cost grows with the size of the collection, and indexing a corpus of about a million tokens took hours in Microsoft’s Graph RAG paper.
A whole-collection question failed in all three setups. “Who works in this group, and what does each person do?” got “the notes do not contain the answer” from simple RAG, --all and the graph walk. No note lists a roster. Microsoft’s Graph RAG builds community summaries for such questions; this toy graph builds none.

One question, one model, one run: this shows the mechanics and does not rank the methods or the models.
Try your own questions and compare.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
A second model: Mistral’s Ministral 3
Swapping the chat model is a one-line change (export CHAT_MODEL=...). ministral-3:8b from Mistral is 6.0 GB on Ollama, supports tools and has an Apache 2.0 licence. Retrieval is the same, since the embedding model is the same. The graph is rebuilt by the new model, so its walk differs: 25 facts from 7 notes, against 40 facts from 8 notes with gemma4:12b-mlx.








Setup
gemma4:12b-mlx
ministral-3:8b




Simple RAG, -k 3
“The notes do not contain the answer.”
Not enough information in the notes.


Simple RAG, -k 5
Yes, re-analysis needed (correct).
No (wrong): says R7 used release 2.4.


--all (every note pasted)
Correct.
Lists the right facts, then No (wrong).


Graph walk
Yes (correct).
Collects the R7 and 2.3 facts, then No (wrong).


Whole-collection question
Not answered.
Not answered.



In the --all run, ministral-3:8b listed R7 using 2.3, which has the bug, then answered No because “no re-analysis was done”. In the -k 5 run it misread the release: the note says 2.3.
The graph build with ministral-3:8b took about a minute, saved 80 facts and returned valid JSON for all twelve notes. show printed a few odd entries: Pipeline 2.3 --has issue fix--> Dana Okafor, a node called Pipeline 2.3 issue, and a User node taken from the safety note. Read show against the notes yourself.
With this model, the right passages reached the prompt in three setups and the final answer was still wrong. Retrieval is one half of the job and the reader model is the other half. Read the notes the answer names and see whether they say what the answer says. Test a model on a few questions whose answers you know before you trust it on new ones. mistral-small (24B, 14 GB) is also on Ollama if you want a larger one to try.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
A note on model size
We did not run LightRAG or Microsoft GraphRAG here; this section summarises what their documentation asks of an Ollama setup. Extraction asks a model to produce well-formed JSON for every chunk. With Ollama, Microsoft GraphRAG users “frequently see issues with malformed responses (especially JSON)”. The LightRAG README calls a 30B-parameter model “a reasonable minimum” for local use, and its programming guide says at least 32B. The 12B model here produced valid JSON for all twelve notes, and show lets you judge the facts. If you try a model under about 7B, read the triples before you trust the answers.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
section: Using a real tool with Ollama
text:
Using a real tool with Ollama
graph.py is a teaching toy. Two real projects do this at scale. Check their current docs before you rely on the details below.
LightRAG (github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG):

Install pip install "lightrag-hku[api]" (the README also shows uv), copy env.example to .env, and run lightrag-server.
For Ollama, the project’s guide wires ollama_model_complete for chat and ollama_embed for embeddings.
LightRAG requires at least 32k context tokens, and Ollama’s default is smaller. Set num_ctx to 32768 in code or in a Modelfile. For the server, set OLLAMA_LLM_NUM_CTX in .env. The default context is 4k on machines under 24 GiB of video memory, so check with ollama ps.
Use a non-thinking model for extraction. Models slower than about 50 tokens per second may time out on dense chunks.
Pick your embedding model before indexing and keep it. EMBEDDING_DIM must equal the model’s output size (the guide uses 768 for nomic-embed-text). Changing the model later means re-embedding everything.
The default storage is in-memory files meant for small tests.
Server safety: lightrag-server binds to all network interfaces with authentication off by default. On a laptop or shared machine, set HOST=127.0.0.1 before you start it.

Microsoft GraphRAG (microsoft.github.io/graphrag):

The commands are graphrag init, graphrag index and graphrag query "..." --method local (or global). Text files go in input/.
It can consume a lot of LLM resources. Start with the small tutorial dataset and cheaper models.
It calls models through LiteLLM and requires structured JSON output. Users put Ollama behind a proxy and report frequent malformed responses. Check the current docs for an Ollama setup.
Check that the embedding vector size in its settings matches your embedding model’s (nomic-embed-text gives 768).

To build a graph over your own notes with Ollama, start with LightRAG on a tiny folder of mock files, then look at the facts it extracted before pointing it at anything real.

title: Grow a Graph with Ollama
text:
Verify the graph
A confident answer built on a wrong link is the failure to look for. A graph gives you a list of facts, each with its source note, to check.

Read the extracted facts for a few notes against the notes themselves. Count the wrong ones.
Ask the agent or the script to name the notes behind each answer, then open them.
Keep a short list of questions whose answers you know, and run it after you change the model, the prompt or the notes.
Keep real and controlled data out of this exercise. The same scripts pointed at a hosted model send every note to that provider.

These notes are mock data, so sending them to a hosted model is fine for this exercise. Check your data agreement before a hosted agent reads your own unpublished notes.
