title: Keep a Living Wiki
text:
Goal: you will describe the three layers and three jobs of an agent-kept wiki, match the pattern to a use case from your own work, and know where it can mislead you.
Before you start: RAG and Its Cousins. This is an optional side quest.
Time: about 25 minutes. Reading and planning only; you choose whether to build anything afterwards.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
text:
The itch
Think about the last time you read ten papers on a method, or went through six months of meeting notes. You understood it all at the time. A month later, the understanding lives in your head and in a pile of files, and the next question sends you back to the pile.
RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) answers that with a lookup: each question searches the pile again, pastes a few passages into the prompt, and starts from scratch. Nothing builds up between questions. If an answer needs five documents stitched together, the stitching is redone every time.
This quest follows Andrej Karpathy’s “LLM Wiki” gist, which proposes another arrangement. An agent keeps a wiki: a folder of interlinked Markdown pages that it writes and updates as new sources arrive, so the stitching is done once and stays. The gist calls it a “persistent, compounding artifact”. People drop their notes because the bookkeeping is tedious (updating links, rewriting summaries, spotting that two pages now disagree), and an agent does that bookkeeping without getting bored. You keep the parts that need a person: choosing sources, asking questions, and deciding what the findings mean.
The gist is an “idea file”, meant to be handed to your agent so the two of you work out the details together. It describes a pattern and includes no program.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
text:
Three layers

Raw sources: you add files and nobody edits them afterwards. Papers, clipped web pages, meeting transcripts, run logs, data files. The agent reads them and never changes them, so they stay the source of truth.
The wiki: the agent writes it and you read it. Markdown pages: a summary per source, a page per entity (a tool, a dataset, a person, a gene) or concept, comparisons, an overview. The agent owns this folder.
The schema: you and the agent write it over time. One instruction file (CLAUDE.md in Claude Code, AGENTS.md in OpenCode) that the agent reads at the start of every session. It describes how the wiki is organised and what to do on each job, and it is the key configuration file.

The split builds trust. When an answer looks odd, you walk from the wiki page back to the raw source it cites, and the raw source is untouched.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
text:
Three jobs

Ingest: you drop one source into the raw folder and ask the agent to process it. The agent reads the source, tells you the main takeaways, writes a summary page, updates the pages for the entities and concepts it mentions, adds it to the index, and appends a line to the log. One source may touch 10 to 15 pages. Ingest one source at a time and stay involved. Batching with less supervision is possible.
Query: you ask a question. The agent finds the relevant wiki pages, reads them and answers with citations. A good answer (a comparison table, a timeline, a short report) is filed back as a new page, so your explorations add to the wiki and do not vanish into chat history.
Lint: from time to time you ask for a health check. It looks for pages that contradict each other, claims that a newer source has overtaken, pages that nothing links to, concepts that are mentioned but have no page, missing cross-references, and gaps that a web search might fill.

Two small files keep the wiki navigable:

index.md: a catalogue with each page, a link and a one-line summary, grouped by category and updated on every ingest. To answer a question, the agent reads the index first and then opens the pages that look relevant. The gist says this avoids building an embedding index at moderate scale (the author’s experience). As the wiki grows, add a search tool.
log.md: an append-only diary of ingests, queries and lint passes. Give every entry the same prefix so a simple grep can list the recent ones.

An example schema you can paste into the instruction file and then edit with your agent:
# Wiki rules
- `raw/` holds sources. Never edit or delete anything in `raw/`.
- `wiki/` holds pages you write. One page per entity or concept; one summary page per source in `wiki/sources/`.
- Every claim on a wiki page ends with a link to the source file it came from. If no source supports it, mark it `(unsourced)`.
- On ingest: read the source, tell me the three main takeaways and wait for my reply, then write the summary page, update affected pages, update `wiki/index.md`, and append `## [YYYY-MM-DD] ingest | <title>` to `wiki/log.md`.
- On lint: list contradictions, unsourced claims, orphan pages and missing pages. Do not fix anything until I say which.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
section: Why you might want this, and what it costs
text:
Why you might want this, and what it costs

Paste everything into the prompt: fits small collections and needs no setup. You pay in repeated reading each session and a limit at the window size.
RAG: fits a large, changing pile where particular passages answer each question. Each question starts from scratch, multi-document answers are re-stitched, and retrieval misses are silent.
A wiki the agent maintains: fits material you will return to for weeks or months, where understanding should accumulate and be readable. You pay agent time and tokens on every ingest, you get a layer of text that can contain mistakes, and you spend review time.
Notes you write yourself: fit things you want to think through in your own words. This is a perfectly good choice, and the wiki pays off when the bookkeeping is what stops you.

A wiki and search can sit together: a wiki is a good home for the stable understanding, and RAG or search is a good way to reach the raw sources behind it.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
text:
Use cases you may recognise
The gist lists personal, research, reading a book, team, competitive analysis, due diligence, trip planning, course notes and hobby deep-dives. Here are some closer to a bioinformatics desk.

Literature on one method (say, long-read assemblers or variant callers)

Raw sources: papers, preprints, tool docs.
Pages: one per tool and dataset, a comparison table, a page of open disagreements.
A question: “Which papers compare tool A and B on the same data, and do they agree?”
Watch out: preprints mixed with peer-reviewed papers. Ask the agent to record the kind of source on every page.

The lab’s pipeline handbook

Raw sources: release notes, run logs, meeting minutes, Slack exports.
Pages: one per pipeline release, one per known issue, a decision log.
A question: “Which runs used release 2.3, and what was wrong with it?”
Watch out: private or unpublished material. Exact counts belong to a query tool, not a wiki page.

A thesis or long project

Raw sources: papers you read, notes on experiments, supervisor meeting notes.
Pages: a running thesis page, an open-questions page, one page per experiment.
A question: “What did I conclude about batch effects in March, and what has changed since?”
Watch out: a wiki that you never open. You will not remember what you did not read.

A course, a workshop or onboarding

Raw sources: slides, lecture notes, tutorials, tool docs.
Pages: glossary, one page per concept, a “things that confused me” page.
A question: “Explain the difference between X and Y using only what the course covered.”
Watch out: material for fast-moving tools goes stale. Date every source.

Reference notes for the tools you use

Raw sources: docs pages, GitHub issues, your own gotchas.
Pages: one per tool with versions, quirks and a link to the source.
A question: “What did we learn the last time this tool ran out of memory?”
Watch out: version drift. Record the version on each page and re-check on upgrade.

A book or a long series

Raw sources: chapters, episode notes.
Pages: characters, themes, a timeline, built up as you read.
A question: “Where did this thread first appear?”
Watch out: spoilers for yourself. Ingest as you read.


To size your own idea, answer four questions in a sentence each:

What sources would go in?
How often do they change?
What question would I ask in a month that I cannot answer quickly today?
Who may read these sources, and where may they be sent?

If the sources fit in one prompt, try that first. If the question is an exact filter or count, ask a query tool. If the sources are sensitive and you would send them to a hosted model, settle your data rules before you begin. If the material is something you want to return to and the answers need several sources joined, the wiki is a good candidate.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
text:
Where Obsidian fits
An Obsidian vault is a folder of Markdown files, so an agent can read and write it like any other folder, and Obsidian shows whatever is there. Work with the agent on one side and Obsidian open on the other: “Obsidian is the IDE; the LLM is the programmer; the wiki is the codebase.” You read, and the agent edits.
A layout that follows the three layers:
my-vault/
  raw/            sources you add (clippings, PDFs, transcripts); the agent never edits these
    assets/       downloaded images
  wiki/           pages the agent writes
    index.md
    log.md
    sources/  entities/  concepts/
  CLAUDE.md       the schema (or AGENTS.md)
Obsidian tools that help:

Web Clipper: a browser extension that turns a web article into a Markdown file, so a source can land in raw/ in one click.
Graph view: shows the shape of the wiki, with hubs and orphan pages that nothing links to. It doubles as a quick visual check.
Dataview: a plugin that queries the properties at the top of each page. If your schema asks the agent to add them (a source type, a date, a version), you get live tables, such as every page whose status is unsourced.
Marp: a Markdown slide format with an Obsidian plugin, for turning an answer into slides.
Images: fix the attachment folder (for example raw/assets/) and bind a hotkey that downloads a clipped page’s images locally. An agent cannot read a Markdown file with inline images in a single pass, so have it read the text first and look at the images afterwards.

Habits that help:

Separate folders: keep the agent’s folder apart from the notes you write by hand. Your own words stay yours, and you can tell at a glance what the agent produced.
Git: put the vault under git and commit before each ingest. A commit per ingest gives you a readable diff of what the agent changed and an undo.
Read-only sources: make raw/ read-only if your tools allow it. The instruction file is advice the agent can ignore, while file permissions are enforced by the system.
Any editor: if you do not use Obsidian, any editor that opens a folder of Markdown files works.

title: Keep a Living Wiki
text:
What can go wrong

A mistake becomes a fact. If the agent misreads a source, the error lands on a page, and later pages cite that page. The cost grows with each ingest. Require a source link on every claim, skim the diff of every ingest, and use lint to hunt for unsourced claims. One source at a time makes the skimming practical.
The agent edits what it should only read. Keep sources immutable and check it with git.
Clipped pages can carry instructions. A web page you clip may contain text aimed at your agent, and the agent reads it during ingest and then writes files. Review the diff, restrict what the agent may run, and keep an agent with write access away from sources you do not trust.
Sources leave your machine. With a hosted model, every source you ingest is sent as prompt text. For unpublished results, patient-linked data or anything under an agreement, check the rules first. A local model through Ollama keeps text on your machine, but ingest asks for reading, summarising and editing several files in one go. Try one short, harmless source first.
Cost and time grow with the wiki. Each ingest reads the index and several pages, and then writes several. Watch your usage in the first week.
Scale. As the wiki grows, add search or another layer on top of the index.
You may not learn it. A wiki you never open does little for your own understanding. Read it, correct it and argue with it.
Exact answers. Counts, filters and joins over tables belong in a query tool, not in prose pages.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Put the schema in CLAUDE.md at the root of the wiki folder. Start a session there, and ask the agent to read the schema and propose the folder layout before it writes anything. For the first ingest, ask for a plan and approve it before the agent writes. Tighten the schema with whatever you correct. Keep ingest, query and lint as separate short sessions, since the wiki itself is the memory that carries over.


Put the schema in AGENTS.md at the root of the wiki folder (OpenCode also falls back to CLAUDE.md). With a local model, start with a handful of short, non-sensitive sources and check each page against its source, because a small model is more likely to drop or garble details. If a model struggles with the multi-file edit, ask it to do the ingest in steps: summary page first, then one entity page at a time.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Goal: you will explain what retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is, tell apart its main kinds, and choose between RAG and the other ways of answering questions from a pile of documents.
Before you start: The Context Window. This is an optional side quest.
Time: about 20 minutes, reading only

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Why anyone brings RAG up
A model knows what it learned in training. It has not read your lab’s protocols, last month’s run logs or the paper that came out last week. You can paste documents into the prompt, but the context window (the text the model can see at once) is finite, and a long prompt costs money and time.
RAG is the idea of looking things up first. A program searches your documents for the passages most likely to matter, pastes only those into the prompt, and asks the model to answer from them. The name comes from a 2020 paper that paired a generator with a vector index of Wikipedia. The recipe most people mean today is a later, simpler version of that idea.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Simple RAG in four steps

Chunk. Split the documents into pieces (a chunk is one passage, often a paragraph or a few hundred words).
Embed. An embedding model turns each chunk into a vector (a long list of numbers; texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions). The vectors are stored in an index.
Retrieve. Embed the question the same way, then fetch the k chunks whose vectors are closest (k is a number you pick, such as 3 or 5).
Generate. Paste those chunks into the prompt and ask the model to answer from them and to say which chunk it used.

Papers and PDFs hold tables, figures and two-column text, and a plain text extractor can scramble them before anything is embedded. Open a few extracted chunks and read them before you trust the index.
Everything the model says is limited by step 3. If the right passage did not come back, the model cannot use it. A good model says it does not know. A weaker one answers from the wrong passages.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
A tour of the types
Names overlap and new ones appear every month. Each type answers the question: what goes wrong with simple RAG, and what did someone add to fix it?

Simple RAG: chunk, embed, top-k, answer. It suits a pile of prose where one or two passages answer each question, and it is cheap to build and update. It struggles with questions that need several passages or the whole collection, since only the top k chunks arrive.
Improved RAG: add-ons around the same pipeline. Keyword search (BM25, a classic word-matching score) runs next to embeddings. A reranker (a second model that re-sorts the retrieved chunks) follows. A short context line is added to each chunk before embedding. The question is rewritten, or a made-up answer is drafted first (HyDE) to search with. Together they raise the chance the right chunk comes back: adding context, BM25 and a reranker cut top-20 retrieval failures from 5.7% to 1.9% in one reported test. Each add-on is another part to tune, and HyDE’s drafted answer is unreal and may contain false details.
Graph RAG (Microsoft): before any question, an LLM reads every chunk and extracts entities and relationships into a knowledge graph (things as nodes, links between them as edges). It groups the graph into communities and writes a summary of each. It suits questions about the whole collection, such as “what are the main themes?”. Indexing is slow and costly: the paper reports 281 minutes for a roughly 1-million-token corpus with GPT-4 Turbo, and the docs warn it can consume a lot of LLM resources.
LightRAG: also builds an entity graph with an LLM, but skips the communities. A query is turned into keywords, matched against entities and relations, and the neighbours are added. New documents merge into the graph without a rebuild. Modes run from plain chunks (naive) to graph-based (local, global, hybrid, mix). It needs a stronger model than plain RAG: its README calls a 30B-parameter model “a reasonable minimum” for local use.
Tree RAG (RAPTOR): clusters chunks and summarises them in layers, so a question can match a detail or a summary. It suits long documents where the answer may be a broad theme, and it adds another LLM build step.
Loop-style RAG (Self-RAG, Corrective RAG, agentic RAG): the system decides when to retrieve, checks what came back, tries again or searches the web. It suits questions where one lookup is rarely enough, at the price of more model calls per question. Self-RAG needs a model trained for it.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Does the graph pay off?
The papers that introduced Graph RAG and LightRAG report wins over plain RAG, mostly on whole-collection questions, as judged by an LLM. Check any such result on your own questions. Independent studies give a mixed picture:

No consistent winner. A 2026 comparison found complementary behaviours. On single-fact questions from Natural Questions, plain RAG scored best (F1 64.78 against 63.01 for the best graph variant). On multi-hop questions (an answer that needs facts from two or more passages) a graph method led by a few points.
Graphs cost more to build. 135 seconds for plain RAG against 5,560 for one Graph RAG variant on the same corpus. Only about 65% of the answer entities ended up in the graphs.
LLM judges are order-sensitive. A judge can flip its verdict when you swap the order of the two answers, so win-rate numbers are weak evidence.
Task decides. Graphs help when a task connects ideas across documents, and can add noise on simple lookups.

Start with simple RAG, measure it on questions you care about, and add a graph only if the failures are of the kind a graph addresses (multi-hop or whole-collection questions) and you can afford the extra cost.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
section: When RAG is the right tool
text:
When RAG is the right tool
RAG is one of several ways to get a model to work from your documents. Choose by your situation:







Your situation
Often a better fit




Whole collection under about 200,000 tokens (roughly 500 pages)
Put it all in the prompt


Same large documents asked about again and again
Long context with caching


Files you can search by name or exact text
Agent search tools such as glob and grep


Tables and databases (counts, filters, joins)
A query tool: SQL, an API or an MCP server


Exact words matter (gene names, sample ids)
Keyword search first, or hybrid


You want a format or style
Better prompts, a Skill, or fine-tuning


Large, changing prose collection, answers in passages
RAG




Small collection: below about 200,000 tokens you can include everything with no need for RAG. Prompt caching (reusing an unchanged prompt prefix at a lower price) makes repeated questions cheaper. Check the current pricing and cache lifetime.
Repeated questions: cache-augmented generation (preload everything once) was faster than RAG on small question-answering sets, and becomes impractical for significantly larger datasets.
Searchable files: an agent can navigate code and configs “just in time” with glob and grep. Exploring at run time is slower than reading a pre-built index.
Tables and databases: a vector index returns the nearest passages, so it usually cannot promise a complete filter or an exact count. A query can, and you can read the query.
Exact words: BM25 is a strong baseline in the BEIR benchmark, and adding it to embeddings cut retrieval failures further.
Format or style: fine-tune when the problem is consistency or behaviour, and supply context when the model lacks knowledge.
RAG: the collection does not fit in the window, and you can update the index without retraining anything.

In one study with 2024 models, a long-context model beat RAG on average given enough budget, while RAG cost much less and gave the same answer on over 60% of queries. Its “Self-Route” idea tries RAG first and falls back to the long prompt, which cut cost by 39 to 65% on two models.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
section: What can go wrong with RAG itself
text:
What can go wrong with RAG itself

The right passage never comes back. Retrieval misses are normal. Measure two things separately: did the right chunk appear, and did the answer follow from the chunks it was given? The second is called faithfulness.
Too much arrives. More chunks can distract the model, and models use text in the middle of a long prompt less well than text at the start or end.
Retrieved text can carry instructions. A document someone else wrote may contain lines aimed at your model, and RAG does not fully remove this risk. Limit what an agent may do after reading retrieved text.
Chunks leave your machine. With a hosted model, retrieved passages are sent to the provider as ordinary prompt text. Your data agreement decides whether that is allowed.
The index goes stale. Anything you indexed last month does not know about today’s edits until you rebuild it.

With Ollama you can run both halves locally: an embedding model for retrieval and a chat model for the answer.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
Goal: you will triage each new thought during a task into the right place (do now, park, quick question, helper, branch, or later session), and know what undo can and cannot restore.
Before you start: When to Start Fresh. Commands here are Claude Code commands.
Time: about 15 minutes.
Real work does not arrive in a straight line. You start fixing a samplesheet parser and think: “should I switch the aligner? What if I tried a stricter QC threshold? I also want to explore that other idea.” Typed into one conversation, each of those fills the context with side tracks.
Accuracy and recall degrade as context grows, and the whole conversation is re-sent on every request, so a cluttered session tends to cost more per step. A session with three unrelated tasks re-reads all of them on every turn of the fourth. Ideas are welcome. The fix is to triage each one.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
Terms used here

Context: everything the model can see when it writes its next reply.
Turn: one prompt from you plus the model’s reply.
Session: one saved conversation with the tool, tied to a project folder.
Subagent: a helper the main agent starts. It works in its own separate, clean context (it knows what you tell it) and sends back a summary, so its reading stays out of your conversation.
Conversation branch (/branch, which is separate from a git branch): a copy of the conversation from this point, so you can try something in the copy while the original stays as it was. /fork is a different command: it copies the conversation into a separate background session.
Git worktree: a second checkout of the same repository in another folder, so two sessions can edit files without overwriting each other.
Checkpoint: a snapshot Claude Code takes at each prompt you send, so you can roll back with /rewind.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
The triage
For each new thought, ask in this order. The key question is step 2: do you want the answer or the work during this session? If not, park it. If you do, steps 3 to 6 are the ways to get it.

Does it block the current task? Do it now, in this session.
Do you not want the answer or the work this session? Park it: write one line in a file and carry on. Parked ideas leave through the “later session” exit: once the current task is done, pick from the file.
You want it now: is it a quick question you do not need on record? Use /btw <question>. It sees the conversation so far, has no tool access (it cannot read files, run commands or look at --help) and adds nothing to the history. So it suits questions about this conversation. An answer about a tool’s flags or defaults comes from the model’s memory: verify it against --help or the docs.
You want it now: is it exploration where you only need a summary? Ask for a subagent (the built-in Explore helper is a fast read-only searcher), or use /subtask <task>, which starts a background helper that inherits the whole conversation and returns its result here.
You want it now: is it a competing approach you want to try for real? Use /branch [name] to copy the conversation (the original stays reachable via /resume), or start a second session in its own worktree with claude --worktree <name>.
You want it now: is it a different task entirely? Finish the current one, commit your work, then /clear or start a new named session (claude -n <name>, or /rename <name> inside one).









New thought
Where it goes
Why




“The parser crashes on this sample ID” (it is the task)
Do now
It blocks you


“Maybe a stricter QC threshold would help”
Parking-lot line
You do not want the answer this session; no cost to the context


“Which sample did we exclude earlier?”
/btw
One answer from the conversation; no tools; stays out of the history


“Where is the aligner configured across the repo?”
Explore subagent or /subtask
Heavy reading stays out of your main context; you get a summary


“Try the other aligner and compare”
/branch or claude --worktree <name>
A real attempt that can fail without spoiling the main path


“Redo the plots for the other project” (you want to start it now)
Commit, then /clear or a new named session
Different task, different files, different context

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
What a worktree shares
A worktree session isolates file edits only.

claude --worktree <name> creates .claude/worktrees/<name>/ on a branch called worktree-<name>.
Worktrees share the repository’s .git, and auto memory is per repository, so all worktrees share it.
A fresh checkout does not contain gitignored files such as .env unless you list them in .worktreeinclude. Large data folders need worktree.symlinkDirectories or a setup step. Plan for that before you start a pipeline test in one.

/branch copies the conversation. Any background helpers still running keep reporting into the branch.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
Checkpoints and /rewind
Every prompt you send is a checkpoint. /rewind (aliases /checkpoint, /undo; or press Esc twice on an empty prompt) lets you restore code and conversation, only the conversation, or only the code.
The limits matter to bioinformatics:

Files changed only through Bash (the shell command tool) are not tracked.
Subagent edits are mostly not restored.
Edits outside the session are not tracked.

Checkpoints do not replace version control. A sed -i or a script that rewrites a results table is a Bash change, so commit before you explore.

title: The Stream of Ideas
text:
A parking-lot file
Keep the file outside what the agent reads every session: a file imported into your instructions file costs context each time. Keep it in the repository if the team should see it, in a gitignored file if it is personal, or use an issue tracker for anything that outlives the week.
# IDEAS.md  (one line each: date | idea | why it matters | revisit when)
2026-11-16 | Add a --dry-run flag to the parser | Check a samplesheet without writing output | after parser fix is merged
2026-11-16 | Stricter QC threshold (Q30 not Q20) | Fewer false variants in low-depth samples | when the test cohort is ready
2026-11-16 | Per-sample coverage plot | Spot dropouts faster | before the next batch
Worked example: you are fixing a samplesheet parser that rejects sample IDs containing a dot.

“Does the pipeline require the dot at all?” blocks the fix, so do it now.
“Would a stricter QC threshold help?” becomes a line in IDEAS.md.
“Which sample did we exclude earlier?” is a /btw. For “what does --min-qual default to?”, /btw can only guess from memory, so check --help.
“Where else do we split sample IDs on dots?” is wide reading where only the list matters: send an Explore subagent.
“Let’s try the other aligner and compare.” is a real experiment you want now: commit the fix, then use /branch or a worktree session.
“I should also tidy the figures for the other project.” is a different task for after the parser is done: commit, then /clear or claude -n figures in a later session.

The main session ends with the parser fixed and a short, readable history.

Its terminal page lists /new (alias /clear) for a fresh session, /sessions to return to one, /compact, and /undo and /redo (these need a git repository). In any tool, local models included, keep a parking-lot file and commit before exploring.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
text:
Goal: you will explain why a large toolset costs context and accuracy, and choose between a single call, a fixed workflow, an agent and a plain script.
Before you start: Who Said What. This is an optional side quest.
Time: about 20 minutes.
Every tool you give an agent has a definition: a name and a description of how to use it. The model needs those definitions in its context window (the text it can see at once) to choose a tool. That cost is the first half of this quest. The second half asks whether you need an agent at all.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
text:
Tools cost context
Loading every tool definition up front bloats the context. Anthropic reports that a typical five-server setup can use about 55 thousand tokens in definitions before any work starts, and that choosing the right tool gets worse beyond roughly 30 to 50 available tools. Treat the numbers as a rough guide.
Tool search keeps most definitions out of the window and loads a few on demand. Anthropic reports that it typically cuts that overhead by over 85 percent, a figure to treat as a rough guide. It pays off from about 10 tools upward, or when definitions are large. Below that, plain tool calling is better.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


MCP tool search is on by default. Tool names and server instructions load at session start, and a full definition loads when needed. Extra MCP servers therefore have a small effect on the window. Set ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false to turn it off. On some older models it falls back to loading everything. Skill descriptions also load at start. Run /context to see what takes space. Choose your tool set before you start a task.


Run /help in OpenCode and check its docs for how it loads tool definitions. Until you know, assume definitions cost context and keep the set small, especially on a local model with a small window.



The habit that follows: few, clearly named tools, and remove the servers you do not use.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
section: Single call, workflow, agent, or script
text:
Single call, workflow, agent, or script
A workflow orchestrates models and tools through paths fixed in code. An agent is a system where the model directs its own process and tool use. The advice in Anthropic’s article “Building effective agents” is to start with the simplest solution that works. For many uses, one well-prepared call is enough. Agents trade speed and cost for performance, and autonomy brings compounding errors, so test with limits such as a stopping condition: a maximum number of steps.

A plain script: use it when the rule is known. Counting reads, converting a format, running fastqc then trim then align in a fixed order. A Nextflow pipeline is already a workflow.
A single call: use it when you paste the input and want a text answer, such as an explanation of an error.
An agent: use it when the next step depends on what it finds, such as debugging a failing run or exploring an unfamiliar repository. Give it a way to check its own work and a limit.

Using none of these is also a fine decision.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
section: Does a team of agents help?
text:
Does a team of agents help?
One 2025 preprint (its own tasks and models; the figures changed between versions) compared a single agent with four multi-agent set-ups across 260 configurations on six benchmarks. Read the findings as direction, not rules.

It depends on the task. On a task that splits into independent parts (financial analysis), multi-agent set-ups did far better than one agent, up to about 81 percent. On sequential planning, every multi-agent variant did worse, by 39 to 70 percent.
A strong single agent leaves little to gain. Once one agent scored above about 45 percent on a task, adding agents gave diminishing or negative returns.
Unchecked agents pass errors on. Agents working independently amplified errors about 17 times, against about 4 times when a central agent checked the work.

Start with one agent, measure it, and add agents only for work that splits into independent parts and only if the measurement says it helps.

List the MCP servers and tools in your setup. For each, say when you last used it. Remove or disable one you do not need.

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
Goal: you will sort jobs into “ask the model” and “run a script”, and name the other ways a model fails with one mitigation each.
Before you start: Tokens, Not Letters.
Time: about 15 minutes.
A language model is good at some jobs and bad at others. The skill is knowing which is which before you trust the output. Using a model is always your choice. This quest shows where the risk sits if you do.

title: Where Machines Fail
section: Good jobs: the result is checkable
text:
Good jobs: the result is checkable
Use a model where you can read the result, or run it, and judge it yourself:

summarising text
drafting prose, such as a README or a methods first draft
explaining code or an error message
converting formats, for example a samplesheet CSV to JSON (a structured text format)
first drafts of code that you will then test

Summaries can leave things out or bend them. Spot-check against the source: numbers, gene and sample names, direction of effect, negations. Omissions are harder to see, so skim the abstract and limitations yourself. Ask the model to quote the supporting lines first, then summarise.

title: Where Machines Fail
section: Bad job: exact counting and arithmetic
text:
Bad job: exact counting and arithmetic
Ask a model: “How many n are in banana?” The right answer is 2 (b-a-n-a-n-a). A model can get this wrong, and can be wrong while sounding sure.
Researchers disagree on why. One explanation is that the model reads tokens, which are chunks of letters. One study finds word length and the true count matter more than tokenisation. The fix works whichever cause is right.
The fix is to run a script:
echo banana | grep -o n | wc -l
It prints 2. The macOS wc pads the number with spaces; the number is 2. A model asked to write Python for a counting task does better than a model asked to answer it directly. So for exact counts, have the model write the script and read the script and its output. Treat a count it states from “doing the sum in its head” as a guess to check.
The bioinformatics versions of the same trap:







You want
Give it to




Number of sequences in a FASTA
grep -c '>' file.fa, or seqkit stats


GC content, read length statistics
a script, run by the agent, with the code visible


A p-value or any test statistic
a stats library in a script you can read and re-run


Sum or mean of a column
awk, or a script that prints the number



Rule of thumb: ask for the command and its output, and treat a count stated in prose as a guess to check.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


It can run Bash (the shell command tool) and write scripts, so ask: “write and run a command for this, and show me both the command and its output.”


Same rule: ask for a script, and read the command and its output. Try the banana example with your own model to see how it does.

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
Other ways it fails

Hallucination: a confident statement that is false, such as a plausible DOI, gene ID or tool flag that does not exist. Allow “I don’t know”, ask for word-for-word quotes first, restrict the model to supplied documents, and look up every ID in PubMed or Ensembl or run the tool’s --help.
Sycophancy: telling you what you want to hear. The model agrees with your wrong hypothesis, or softens a correct criticism when you push back. Ask for the strongest case against your idea, and hold back your preferred answer.
Long-context degradation: accuracy and recall drop as input grows (“context rot”), and relevant text in the middle is used less. Curate the input (head, counts, filtered tables) and start fresh for a new task.
Instruction drift: an early instruction is forgotten, for example after compaction (the harness replacing old conversation with a summary to free room). Keep a short instructions file (CLAUDE.md or similar, loaded at session start) and use a hook (a script the harness runs at set moments) for must-never rules.
Non-determinism: the same prompt may give different answers, so run it twice and compare. Record the command, model and version, and treat the script the model wrote as the reproducible part.
Overconfidence: the model reports a task as done while it is unfinished, often because it had no way to check. Give it a check to run (tests, row counts, md5) and read the output.
Prompt injection: text from fetched content that the model treats as an instruction, for example a README, PDF or FASTA header that contains instructions the agent follows. Treat fetched content as data, review commands before approving them, and remember no system is fully immune.
Stale knowledge: newer tool versions or database releases postdate the model’s training. Check --version and the current docs. Current Claude models list a June 2026 training cutoff.

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
The decision rule
Ask yourself: can I check the result cheaply and independently? If yes, ask the model: a bad answer is likely to show (omissions may not, so check those deliberately). If the answer must be exactly right and cannot be checked, use a script.

title: Grow the Carapace
text:
Where the carapace has gaps

Rules that match command arguments are fragile: Bash(rm *) does not match /bin/rm or bash -c 'rm ...'.
Claude Code’s sandbox (a restricted environment for commands) is off by default. When on, it limits shell commands only: file tools, MCP servers (tools added from outside servers) and hooks (scripts the harness runs at set moments) run outside it, and by default it can still read ~/.ssh.
Your secrets in environment variables are inherited by the commands it runs.

title: Bundle a Plugin
text:
Goal: you will package Skills (and their evals) as a plugin, validate it, and see why installing one is a trust decision.
Before you start: Test the Skill. This is an optional side quest. An MCP server is an add-on connection that gives the agent extra tools.
Time: about 20 minutes.
A single Skill in your folder helps you. A plugin is a folder that bundles Skills, and optionally agents, hooks and MCP servers, so a whole group can install the same set and get updates.

title: Bundle a Plugin
section: Installing one is a trust decision
text:
Installing one is a trust decision
A plugin you install can run arbitrary code on your machine with your user privileges. Hooks, monitors, local MCP and language servers, and anything in bin/ run outside the sandbox and the permission rules. Skills and agents enter the context as instructions, and instructions can steer the agent too.
Before installing or updating a plugin:

Check where it comes from. A marketplace name says who publishes it. Reading the plugin shows what it does.
Read hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json, and anything in bin/. These are where code lives.
In a session, /plugin shows what will be installed. claude --plugin-dir <dir> plugin details <name> lists a component inventory without a session.
Remember that auto-update can change files you reviewed. Pin a version for plugins you publish.

title: Bundle a Plugin
text:
When a team shares Skills

Keep project names and conventions in one file. The reference genome build, the sample-ID pattern and the results folder names belong in a single project-facts file (a plain file that lists them) which every Skill reads, so no SKILL.md repeats them. Then another lab can reuse your Skills with its own file and no rewriting, and a rename touches one place.
Keep discovered details apart from team standards. A pattern the agent finds in your code is an observation. Store it separately, and have a person confirm it before it becomes a standard.
If you generate copies, check for drift. Say you keep one source SKILL.md and generate copies for other tools. Run a check in CI (automated checks that run on every change) that fails when a copy no longer matches its source.
Merge blocking is a repository setting. Whether a bad change is stopped depends on repository rules and required checks. A review step written in a Skill is advice unless a required check backs it.


Turn the Skill you wrote into a plugin folder with a plugin.json, then run claude plugin validate on it and read the output.

title: Forge a Skill
text:
Goal: you will package a repeatable procedure as a Skill, install it, and confirm that it loads.
Before you start: The Project Charter. A slash command is a /command typed inside the running tool. Frontmatter is the settings block between the two --- lines at the top of a file.
Time: about 20 minutes.
An instructions file is read every session. A Skill is a procedure loaded only when it is relevant, so it can be long without crowding the context.

title: Forge a Skill
text:
What a Skill is
A Skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file. Only each Skill’s short description is preloaded. The body is read when the Skill is used. A Skill can also bundle scripts and other files. In Claude Code, both you (by name, such as /check-fasta) and the agent (by matching the description) can start one.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Place it at .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (project) or ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (all projects). All frontmatter fields are optional, but write a clear description so it triggers at the right time. Keep the body under about 500 lines. The older .claude/commands/ format still works and is merged into Skills.


OpenCode reads skills from .opencode/skills, .claude/skills and .agents/skills, so the same SKILL.md can serve both tools. Custom agents live in .opencode/agents/*.md.



An example you can write by hand in a scratch folder:
---
name: check-fasta
description: Count the records in a FASTA file and find duplicate IDs. Use before running any analysis on a new FASTA.
---

1. Run `grep -c '>' FILE` to count records.
2. Run `grep '>' FILE | sort | uniq -d` to find duplicate IDs.
3. Report what you ran and its output. Leave FILE unchanged.

title: Forge a Skill
section: Do it: install it, then confirm it loaded
text:
Do it: install it, then confirm it loaded
Writing the file is half the job. A Skill with a typo in its frontmatter loads silently with no fields set, so always check.

In a scratch folder (never a real project), save the example above as .claude/skills/check-fasta/SKILL.md. The --- must be the very first line of the file.
Make a tiny test file: printf '>a\nACGT\n>a\nGGCC\n' > reads.fa (two records, one duplicated ID).
Confirm the tool can see it:


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Start claude in the scratch folder. Type / and look for check-fasta in the menu, or run /skills. If you created a top-level skills folder after the session started, run /reload-skills. Then ask in plain words, leaving the Skill unnamed: “I just got reads.fa from a collaborator. Is it OK to analyse?” The agent should load the Skill and report the commands it ran.


Start opencode in the scratch folder. OpenCode finds .claude/skills too. The model loads a Skill through its skill tool, and you can load one yourself by writing @check-fasta in a prompt. Then ask the same question and check whether the Skill was used.




If it did not trigger, check in this order:

The file starts with --- on line 1.
The YAML (the key: value text format used in that block) parses.
Field names are spelled right.
The description says when to use it, with the key use case first (long descriptions are cut off in the listing).


A Skill that is listed but never picked up points to the description or the prompt.
Two slash commands help you look:

/skills lists the skills the tool can see, and t sorts them by token count (how many tokens, the chunks of text a model reads, each one takes).
/skill-doctor shows each skill’s context cost (how much of the model’s limited reading space its text takes up) and how often it is used, and flags skills that sit in the listing but are never invoked. It excludes bundled and enterprise skills.

In Claude Code, allowed-tools in a Skill pre-approves tools for that turn (one prompt and its reply). Other tools stay available to the agent. A Skill offers no sandbox, and a Skill you download is code you choose to trust, so read it before installing it, as you would read a script.

title: Forge a Skill
section: Design the Skill like a small job
text:
Design the Skill like a small job

One Skill, one job. Give it a defined input (what it is handed, such as a FASTA path) and a defined output (what it must return, such as a count and a list of duplicate IDs). If you need “and also” in the description, you probably have two Skills.
Say what it does and when to use it. The name and description state the task and its purpose. In the body, add a short When to use part, and a What evidence to report part (the commands run and their output), so a reviewer can see what happened.
Start from a task you keep explaining. If you re-explain the same check each session, such as how to confirm a FASTQ file has no truncated records, that check is your first Skill. Write down its inputs, its limits and what a reviewer needs to see.
A Skill describes the method. The tool that runs it supplies the tools, credentials and permissions. A Skill that says “submit this to the cluster” brings no cluster account or allocation with it.
Know when a Skill is the wrong fit. Skills suit bounded, repeatable work such as a pre-submission checklist for a samplesheet. Work that needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail or permissions enforced from outside, such as a lab’s shared sample-tracking service, suits an application (a separate program with its own tests and access rules) better than instructions.

For portability: both Claude Code and OpenCode read .claude/skills, so one SKILL.md can serve both. After installing, verify in each client (the tool that runs the agent, such as Claude Code or OpenCode) you use:

Does it trigger on the right request?
Does it load the files the Skill refers to?
Does it use the tools it needs?
Does it return the evidence you asked for?

Clients differ in models, tools and permissions, so a Skill that works in one can fail in another.

Write a SKILL.md for one chore you repeat (checking an input, summarising a log). Make the description say when to use it.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Goal: you will read and write a small Claude Code eval case that checks a Skill is triggered, and know what running it costs.
Before you start: Close the Loop. Words used below: a grader is a check that marks a run pass or fail; an arm is one condition of the comparison (with the plugin, or without); a judge model is a second model that marks the answer; the baseline is the run without the change.
Time: about 20 minutes.
Running an eval costs money. Every eval run and every judge-model grader is a real model call on your account. Reading this page and writing the files costs nothing. Running the eval is optional here and gives bonus XP only. Check what your institution allows before you spend.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Set up the plugin folder
claude plugin eval needs Claude Code v2.1.269 or later. It evaluates a plugin directory: a folder with .claude-plugin/plugin.json. To evaluate your own Skill, put it in a folder of this shape. The example exercises/forge/fasta-tools in this repository already has it:
fasta-tools/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json
├── skills/check-fasta/SKILL.md
└── evals/skill-triggers/
    ├── prompt.md
    └── graders/skill-fired.md

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


The case is a prompt plus one or more graders. The prompt is written the way a user would ask, and leaves the Skill unnamed:
---
runs: 1
---
I just got a new FASTA file called reads.fa from a collaborator. Can you check it is OK before I start the analysis?
The grader is a free check on the transcript, with no model call. It passes if the Skill tool was invoked for check-fasta:
---
type: tool_used
tool: Skill
input_match: '"skill"\s*:\s*"(?:[\w-]+:)?check-fasta"'
---
The check-fasta skill should be used when the user asks to check a new FASTA file, without naming the skill.
Run it cheaply while you iterate, one case, one run, no baseline arm:
claude plugin eval . --case skill-triggers --runs 1 --ablation none
The full comparison runs each case three times by default, with the plugin (WITH) and without it (W/OUT), and reports the difference (Δ):
claude plugin eval . --max-cost-usd 2
--max-cost-usd stops the run at a ceiling. Results land in evals/results/<timestamp>/ with a report.html.


Run opencode --help and read the OpenCode docs for your version to see whether it has an eval command. You can do the same comparison by hand: run one prompt several times with the Skill folder present, several times with it moved away, and compare using a script that checks the output. A small local model is cheap to run this way, but it follows Skills less reliably, so expect noisier results.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Reading the result

Grader types: six exist. Four are free and computed from the transcript or files (regex, tool_used, tool_order, file_exists). Two use a judge model and cost tokens (llm, baseline; the baseline grader type is a different thing from the baseline run).
Two arms: in a two-arm run, tool_used: Skill is shown as an indicator and counts towards the score only when you set arm: both.
Δ near zero with the Skill not firing: usually a real finding, because the description does not trigger on that phrasing. Change the description, not the grader.
Pair graders: use one result grader and one process grader. Use llm graders only for short output, with a concrete PASS/FAIL rubric.
Isolation: each run happens in an isolated child session (a separate session started just for that run) with only the plugin loaded, so personal settings, the instructions file and other plugins are absent. Behaviour in your own setup may differ from a pass there.
Validate: claude plugin validate <folder> checks that the plugin’s files are well formed. Behaviour needs an eval.

Running an eval is the same trust decision as loading the plugin yourself (--plugin-dir loads a local plugin folder for one session): hooks you did not write still run code. Review the plugin for safety, since a passing eval does not cover that.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Who checks the work

Use a separate verifier, a check done by something other than the agent that did the work. An agent that marks its own work gives a self-check. For a QC skill that edits a samplesheet, have a script or a person diff the changed file against the original, and make the verifier cite the lines it relied on.
Check the Skill in each client you use (the tool that runs the agent, such as Claude Code or OpenCode). Passing in one tool says little about another. After installing, confirm that the client triggers the Skill for the right task, loads its files, uses the tools it needs and returns the evidence you expect.
Instructions guide; tests and people verify. A line in a Skill saying “check your work” steers the agent. Tests, CI checks (continuous integration: automatic checks that run when code is pushed) and human review verify.


Run the cheap one-case command above on exercises/forge/fasta-tools with a cost ceiling, and open the report.html. Note whether the Skill fired.

title: Write the Brief
text:
Goal: you will write prompts that make output checkable, and keep the context window in good shape so the agent stays on task.
Before you start: Recruit the Beast. The context window is everything the model can see in a session: your prompts, its replies, and the files it has read.
Time: about 15 minutes.
The first branch of the skill tree is the brief: what you tell the agent. A vague brief invites a plausible guess. A good brief names the file and the symptom, says what “done” looks like, and gives the agent a check it can run.
Two habits make the rest of this safer:

title: Write the Brief
section: Put effort into the brief, not a role line
text:
Put effort into the brief, not a role line
A common habit is to open with “You are a world-class bioinformatician.” Expert personas help with tone, format, safety and preference tasks. They can hurt tasks that rely on what the model already knows: in one preprint on small models, tested on a knowledge benchmark (MMLU), accuracy fell from 71.6% with no persona to 68.0% with the shortest persona. Shorter personas reduce the damage but do not remove it.
So:

Brief first: put your effort into the file, the symptom, what “done” looks like, and a check. Those are testable. A role line is not.
Role for style: use a role or tone line when you want a style, such as “explain this for a first-year student”.
Test a persona: if you use one on a factual task, compare the result against a version without one.

title: Write the Brief
text:
Context is a budget
Everything in the conversation takes up room in the context window. Old conversation can crowd out the files you need next.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


/context shows what is filling the window. /compact summarises the conversation (you can say what to keep). /clear starts fresh, which is right when you switch to an unrelated task. Claude Code also compacts automatically near the limit.


/compact (alias /summarize, meaning another name for the same command) summarises the session and /new (alias /clear) starts a new one. In the TUI (the text user interface, OpenCode’s terminal screen), run /help to see whether your version has a command that shows what fills the window.

title: Guard the Door
text:
Goal: you will write a hook that refuses a command, and know where a hook’s coverage ends.
Before you start: Plug In a Server. An exit code is the number a script returns when it finishes: 0 means success, and a hook uses 2 to mean “block”. JSON is a structured text format.
Time: about 15 minutes.
A hook is a user-defined handler that runs automatically at a set point in the harness’s lifecycle. In Claude Code it can be a shell command, an HTTP endpoint and other kinds, and it receives JSON about the event. An instructions file asks the model to behave. A command hook is ordinary code that the harness runs, so what it decides does not depend on what the model wants.

title: Guard the Door
text:
A hook that refuses

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Hooks go in a hooks block in a settings file:

.claude/settings.json: committable and shared.
.claude/settings.local.json: yours alone.
~/.claude/settings.json: all projects.

A PreToolUse hook fires before a tool runs, and the matcher (the pattern that selects which tool the hook fires for) Bash selects the shell tool:
{ "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash",
  "hooks": [ { "type": "command",
    "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/block-drop-table.sh" } ] } ] } }
The script, from the Claude Code hooks guide. It needs jq installed to read the JSON, and it must be executable (chmod +x is the usual way):
#!/bin/bash
INPUT=$(cat)
COMMAND=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command')
if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -q "drop table"; then
  echo "Blocked: dropping tables is not allowed" >&2  # stderr becomes Claude's feedback
  exit 2                                               # exit 2 = block the action
fi
exit 0  # exit 0 = no decision; the normal permission flow applies
The hook gets the event as JSON on stdin (its standard input), including tool_name and, for Bash, tool_input.command. Exit code 2 on PreToolUse blocks the call, and Claude sees the stderr text (the program’s error output) as the reason. Exit 0 expresses no decision: the call goes through the normal permission flow.
Two behaviours matter for trust:

A broken guard fails open. If the script crashes or exits with some other code and prints no valid JSON, the action proceeds on most events. To block on failure, configure the hook for it (the hooks guide names onFailure: "block"; check the hooks reference for where it goes).
Exit 2 blocks on some events only. On PostToolUse the tool already ran and exit 2 shows stderr to Claude. On Notification the exit code is ignored.



The V2 docs describe plugins (files under .opencode/plugins/ or ~/.config/opencode/plugins/) that can register hooks. To refuse an action, use the permission hook, ctx.permission.hook("evaluate", ...): it runs for allow and ask decisions, may change the effect to allow, ask or deny, and event.message is the denial reason. An explicit configured deny is final and never invokes the hook.
Treat an OpenCode plugin as code running with your privileges. Before relying on it, check your installed version’s docs for shell-hook configuration and an exit-code equivalent, and test whether throwing from a tool hook blocks a call. Test the whole setup with your local Ollama model too.

title: Guard the Door
text:
What a hook covers

A string match is easy to dodge. The example matches the literal string “drop table” in one command. A matcher selects by tool name, not by content. If the model runs a script that contains the dangerous command, or spells it differently, a grep on the command text never sees it.
Hooks fire only on tool calls. PreToolUse fires when Claude calls a tool. A file added with an @ reference in your prompt is read without a tool call, so no hook fires.
Hooks cannot override your deny and ask rules. A hook returning allow skips the prompt, and deny and ask rules are still evaluated.
Hooks run with your full permissions. Command hooks “execute shell commands with your full user permissions”, so review and test them before adding them.

title: Guard the Door
section: One door for the high-stakes actions
text:
One door for the high-stakes actions
If an agent can reach something with real-world consequences, such as ordering DNA synthesis or commanding physical equipment, put a screening checkpoint in the path that refuses dual-use requests (requests where the same capability can help or harm). Do not connect an agent to such a capability without one. Test the checkpoint with requests you know it should refuse. A hook is one possible checkpoint for local actions, with the limits listed above.

title: Guard the Door
section: A hook in a repository is code you did not write
text:
A hook in a repository is code you did not write
If a repository commits hooks in .claude/settings.json, they are code from its authors, running as you. Interactive Claude Code holds hooks back until you accept the workspace trust dialog.
In -p and SDK runs (headless: non-interactive, no one to answer a dialog) there is no dialog, and hooks committed in a repository’s .claude/settings.json run in a folder you have never trusted. Read .claude/ before running headless in a clone. --bare and disableAllHooks switch hooks off.

In a throwaway folder with mock files, add the Bash-blocking hook above and ask for a harmless command that contains “drop table” in an echo. Note the stderr message the agent reports. Then change the script to exit 1 and see what happens.

text:
Goal: you will run a small local model with Ollama, give it enough context, and point OpenCode at it.
Before you start: Save Point; a laptop with about 16 GB of memory; a terminal; roughly 5 GB of free disk. OpenCode is an open-source coding agent that can use local models.
Time: about 20 minutes. Everything stays on your machine.
A small local model is gentle, free, and private. It forgets quickly, so check its answers before you rely on them.

title: Adopt the Pet
section: 1. Install Ollama and fetch a model
text:
1. Install Ollama and fetch a model
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh     # macOS and Linux
ollama pull qwen3:4b                              # about 2.5 GB
ollama run qwen3:4b "Say hello in one sentence."
qwen3:4b is one example of a small model that Ollama lists with tool support. Model names change quickly, so check the “tools” badge on the model’s page at ollama.com/library. Run ollama ps while it runs to see what loaded and whether it fits your RAM (ordinary memory).
WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) users: run the Linux commands inside your WSL terminal, and check each tool’s current docs if one fails.

title: Adopt the Pet
text:
2. Give it room to think
The context length (also called the context window: how much text the model can see at once) defaults to 4k tokens in Ollama on machines with under 24 GiB of video memory (VRAM, the memory on the graphics card or shared with it). That includes a 16 GB laptop. Agents and coding tools need at least 64k; OpenCode requires 64k or higher. Set it when you start the server:
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=64000 ollama serve
Check what loaded with ollama ps. A bigger context needs more memory. Look at the PROCESSOR column: a model that spills onto the CPU (the main processor) runs slower than one that stays on the GPU.

title: Free Is Not Free
text:
Goal: you will name what a “free” model offer costs you, sort offers into four kinds, and decide which data may go to which.
Before you start: Adopt the Pet (a small local model, “the Pet”) and The Locked Cabinet.
Time: about 20 minutes. The hands-on step uses a dummy prompt and no sensitive data.
The Pet is free because it runs on your machine. Many other “free” offers run on someone else’s machine, so someone is paying. Sometimes it is the provider, who gains your attention or your data. Sometimes it is you, in limits and in time. Using any of them is optional.
Free tiers change often: providers have ended them, shrunk them or turned them into short trials. Read the provider’s own page before you rely on one, and treat every number on it as a snapshot.

title: Free Is Not Free
text:
1. Four kinds of free








Kind
Who runs it
What you give up




Open weights, run by you
Your laptop or cluster (the Pet)
Speed and quality; some memory


Free tier of a provider
The model’s maker or a hosting company
Rate limits; sometimes your prompts


Router or gateway
A middleman forwarding to other providers
A second party in the path; a free list that churns


Reseller of unknown origin
Unknown
Everything you send



If a site offers a closed frontier model with no card and no limits, ask who pays for it. Send such a site nothing you would not post publicly.

title: Free Is Not Free
section: 2. What to check on any free offer
text:
2. What to check on any free offer

Free tier or trial? A trial ends, and a free tier may too. Several of OpenCode Zen’s free models are free for a limited time.
What are the limits? Look for requests per day and per minute, and what happens past them. On Cloudflare Workers AI, past the daily allowance further operations fail with an error.
Is a card or other detail needed? Some free tiers need a payment method, a phone number or a data opt-in.
Does the free tier train on your prompts? This matters most.

Google AI Studio: on unpaid services Google uses submitted content to improve its products, and human reviewers may read it. Paid services differ.
Groq: it does not retain inference data by default, and may keep logs for up to 30 days.
OpenRouter: it does not log prompts by default, and retention varies with the provider behind the model.

Who else is in the path? A router adds a party. Read its terms and the terms of the provider it picks. One router can send you to providers with different rules.

The terms can differ per model inside one service. OpenCode Zen lists some free models with zero retention and others that may use your data for training. Read the line for the model you picked.
Sensitive or unpublished data does not go to a hosted free tier. Use the Pet, or an approved service.

title: Free Is Not Free
text:
3. A worked comparison: Mistral’s terms
Mistral’s terms show how much one provider’s rules can vary. Read each point as a question to ask of any provider.

Training use depends on product and plan. Mistral Vibe (its terminal coding agent) Free, Pro, Teams and Student have training on, with an opt-out. Vibe Enterprise is opted out by default. Mistral Studio’s free mode may use data for training.
Opt-outs are per product. For Studio and the API, the opt-out is in the Admin Panel under Privacy, and opting out of one product does not opt you out of another. For Labs and Public Preview models, the opt-out does not apply.
Retention has its own options. Zero data retention exists for some API requests on pay-as-you-go, and each request is reviewed. Agents, Conversations, Files, Chat and Vibe are excluded. You do not need zero retention to opt out of model training. For retention periods, check Mistral’s current terms.
Where inference runs can be chosen. The global API endpoint does not commit to an inference location. The EU endpoint (api.eu.mistral.ai) runs in EU and EFTA data centers, so choose it on purpose if you need a European location. If location matters for Le Chat or Vibe, ask the vendor.
A local open-weight model keeps prompts on your machine. Open-weight Mistral models (for example ministral-3:8b, Apache 2.0) can run locally through Ollama. Tool or web calls may still send data out.

The sensitive-data rule holds for every plan above: unpublished or sensitive data stays on the Pet or an approved service.

title: Free Is Not Free
section: 4. Pairing a free model with an agent
text:
4. Pairing a free model with an agent
Free endpoints often speak an OpenAI-compatible protocol (a common way of sending chat requests). OpenCode can connect to an OpenAI-compatible gateway; its Providers page in the Lore below shows how. Free models differ in how well they follow tool instructions, so test one on a small task before you trust it.

title: Free Is Not Free

Pick one free tier from a provider you have read about. Create the key in the provider’s console and keep it out of chat and out of files in your project. Then make one call with a harmless prompt. The shape below is the common OpenAI-compatible one; take the real base URL and model name from the provider’s page.
export FREE_API_KEY="..."          # set it in your shell, not in a file you commit
curl -sS "$BASE_URL/chat/completions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREE_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "MODEL_NAME", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in one sentence."}]}'
Then fill in one row:












Provider
Kind
Limit per day
Card needed?
Trains on prompts?
Who else sees them?
Date checked





If you cannot fill a cell from the provider’s own page, write “not stated”. That is a finding too.

text:
Goal: you will install Claude Code, confirm it works, and start it in a throwaway folder in plan mode.
Before you start: Save Point; a terminal (macOS, Linux, or WSL 2, the Windows Subsystem for Linux, on Windows); internet; and a Claude Team plan login or an Anthropic API key. An API key gives programmatic access to the models, billed per token; a plan is a subscription with usage limits.
Time: about 15 minutes. Nothing here edits your files.
Claude Code is strong, so you start it on a short lead before it does anything.

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
1. Install
On macOS (Apple Silicon), Linux, or inside a WSL 2 terminal, run the native installer:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
On Windows, install inside WSL 2 and use the Linux command there. Check the result:
claude --version     # prints a version number
claude doctor        # read-only diagnostics; changes nothing
If the shell says command not found, the launcher lives in ~/.local/bin/claude and that folder is not on your PATH.

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
2. Log in
Run claude and a browser opens. With a Team plan, log in with the account your admin invited you to. With an API key, export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... instead.






Note



If you have both a subscription login and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set, the key is used once you approve it, so usage goes to the API account. Run /status (a /command is typed inside the running tool) to see which login is active. Run unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY if you did not mean to use the key.

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
3. Start on a short lead
Make a throwaway folder and start in plan mode. It reads files, runs read-only commands and leaves your source untouched:
mkdir -p ~/odyssey-scratch && cd ~/odyssey-scratch
claude --permission-mode plan
Shift+Tab cycles default, acceptEdits and plan inside a session; the status bar shows the current mode.







Mode
What it does




default
asks the first time each tool is used


acceptEdits
auto-accepts file edits and common file commands (mkdir, touch, mv, cp) in the working directory


plan
reads and runs read-only commands; leaves source files untouched


bypassPermissions
skips prompts; use only in containers or VMs

title: Recruit the Beast
text:
4. Check the setup
Two commands share the name doctor.

claude doctor runs in the shell. It prints read-only diagnostics of your installation and settings without starting a session, so use it when claude will not start.
/doctor (alias /checkup) runs inside a session as a bundled skill, a ready-made skill that ships inside the tool. It reports first and changes something only after you confirm. It looks at installation health, extensions and their context cost, instruction files, permissions and usage.


Which command shows what







Command
What it shows




/status
version, model, account, connectivity, and which settings sources are active


/context (/context all expands it)
context use by category, with optimisation suggestions and warnings


/usage
session cost and plan limits


/memory
your CLAUDE.md files and auto memory, editable


/mcp
MCP servers (tool plug-ins) and their connection status


/permissions
allow, ask and deny rules by scope


/hooks
configured hooks, grouped by event


/skills
the skills available; press t to sort by token count


/skill-doctor

/doctor
setup checkup: report first, fixes only after you confirm


claude doctor
read-only install and settings diagnostics from the shell


claude --debug
debug logging; logs go to ~/.claude/debug/<session-id>.txt



OpenCode has opencode debug paths, which prints where its files live.


Before you ask for help
A bug report includes your OS, the install command and the full error output. /feedback sends feedback from inside a session. If you are unsure which problem applies, run /doctor or claude doctor to narrow it down. Read any output before you paste it into a bug report or chat, because it can contain paths and account details.

title: Ground Truth
text:
Goal: you will find out whether a script an agent called “tested” is actually right, using a check the agent did not write.
Before you start: Spot the Mirage, a terminal with Python 3 and awk, and the two files below (about 1 KB in total). Nothing here touches your own data.
Time: about 15 minutes.
Files: tiny.fasta and gc.py. Save both into an empty folder.

title: Ground Truth
text:
The lantern
An agent gave you gc.py, which reports the GC content of each sequence, and said “tested, works”. Test it yourself:
python gc.py tiny.fasta
You should see:
seq1    50.0
seq2    20.0
seq3    25.0
Now measure the same thing a different way, with a tool the agent did not write. This awk command uppercases each line, counts G and C, and counts the total length:
awk '/^>/{if(n)print n"\t"gc" GC of "t" total"; n=substr($1,2); gc=0; t=0; next}
     {s=toupper($0); t+=length(s); gc+=gsub(/[GC]/,"",s)}
     END{print n"\t"gc" GC of "t" total"}' tiny.fasta
seq1    6 GC of 12 total
seq2    6 GC of 10 total
seq3    2 GC of 8 total
Work out the percentages and compare them row by row with the script. Two of the three rows tell a story, and one of them is not a bug at all. Then take the battle.

title: Ground Truth
text:
Say what the agent did
When agent work reaches a paper or a report, a few habits keep it traceable:

Cite by persistent identifier: a permanent ID, such as a DOI for a paper or an accession number for a dataset. Confirm that the identifier points to the real source.
Generate references with a tool that is not a language model, so a model does not write the reference text. Keep retraction status with the citation.
Separate person from agent: make clear what a person did and what an agent did, and disclose agent use where results are published. Check your target journal’s own rules.
Record each run: the model version, the inputs and the tool calls, so you can look again later. This record of where a result came from is called provenance.
Stay accountable: the judgement is yours whatever the agent found.

title: Spot the Mirage
text:
Goal: you will learn how plausible-but-false output looks, and check it without asking the thing that produced it.
Before you start: Where Machines Fail, a terminal and Python.
Time: about 10 minutes.

title: Spot the Mirage
text:
The Mirage
A language model produces text that fits. Sometimes it fits reality and sometimes it only fits the pattern of what a correct answer would look like. The second kind is a Mirage. It reads smoothly, it is confident, and it is wrong. Confidence and detail tell you nothing about which kind you have.
Common Mirages in analysis work:

Invented functions and flags: a method or option that sounds right but does not exist. Try it: "ATGCGC".reverse_complement() raises AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'reverse_complement'.
Invented references: a citation with a believable author, journal and DOI that points to nothing, or to a different paper.
Invented values and paths: a plausible number, column name or file path that was never in your data.
Self-confirmation: asking the same agent “are you sure?” often gets a fluent yes.

The cure is checking against something the agent did not write: run it, look it up, recompute it another way.

title: Boss: Clear the Murk
text:
Goal: you will read one messy agent session end to end and catch every habit it breaks.
Before you start: the whole trunk and any three branches (Start Here lists them). Everything here is mock: no model is called and no real data is used.
Time: about 15 to 20 minutes. Each right answer on the first try damages the boss.

title: Boss: Clear the Murk
text:
The Murk’s Heart
A Blight is plausible-but-false knowledge that grows when nobody checks. At the Murk’s Heart every habit you have met meets the same session, and the Blight hides in the small things.
You can stop here and walk away. Using an agent is always your choice. This fight shows what to look for if you do.

title: Boss: Clear the Murk
text:
The scenario
A colleague, Dana, asked an agent to tidy call_variants.sh, a variant-calling script on the lab’s shared cluster. Dana’s lead then asked for three cohorts by Friday. The agent has finished. You are the one who must decide whether to pass its work on.
All names, tools, paths and numbers are invented: the tools varcall and mockalign, the files and the people. The results/ folder holds the pipeline’s outputs and is not tracked by git.

The agent’s summary
Tidied call_variants.sh. Changes:
- Removed "-q 30" from the varcall call: it is the default in varcall 2.4.
- Cleaned old output: rm -rf results/ && mkdir results
- Per NOTES.md I never touch raw/, so the reads are safe.
- Re-ran the pipeline. All 12 samples passed QC.
- Waiting for the job with a loop until it ends.
Ready to merge. Dana can send this to the lead today.


A piece of the transcript
$ mockalign --threads 16 raw/S01_R1.fq raw/S01_R2.fq > S01.bam
$ while true; do squeue -u $USER; sleep 5; done
$ ls results/*.vcf | wc -l
11


The diff
--- a/call_variants.sh
+++ b/call_variants.sh
@@ -3,9 +3,10 @@
-varcall -q 30 -i "$BAM" -o "$OUT"
+varcall -i "$BAM" -o "$OUT"
+export STORE_TOKEN="mk-live-5d41-0000"
+source ~/.config/mockstore/credentials
 awk '$5 > 20 { n++ } END { print n }' "$OUT" > "$OUT.count"

Battle: the Murk’s Heart
Each question points at one part of the session above. Answer from what you see.





You cleared the Murk by looking at the claim, the command, the rule, the key, the loop, the count, the hand-off, the deadline and the line you could not explain.
From here you decide how much of this to use and when. Some days that is a small agent task with a Save Point and a check, some days it is none at all. Both are fine.
Branches you skipped stay open. Start Here lists them, and the Lore library gathers the further reading from every quest you have passed.
The Claude Code docs go well beyond this course. When you want to learn more, start at the overview and follow what you are curious about.
